_ IN Cora, the crier of the Court, anxious to dis- perse the crowd around the bar, exclaimed, "All ye blackgnards that isn't lawyers, quit the Court." ACCORDING to the decision of a Kansas judge, both husband and wife are entitled to enter a place of amusement on a ticket reading "Admit one." _

"WHY do you call that dog 'Bo- bby,' old man?" "He's so infernally stupid." "I don't see the con- nection," "Why, London detectives are called bobbies,' you know." He—" I see Miss Jones's back flora Paris." She (a spirited rival)—" I noticed her dress was cut rather low, but I didn't suppose you could see her back from that distance." SOME one is always wanting special legislation. Here come a Connecticut man advocating the passage of a law compelling railway restaurant keepers to date their apple pies and sandwiches. "DID you ever shoot a cross-bowl" asked an enthusiastic archer of Miss Ethelimia." "Ever shoot a cross beau?" she replied. "I should say I had. George got so cross last night that I fired him right out of the house."

Mns. DUSENBERRY (sobbing)—" Oh, it is just dreadful to be disappointed in love !" Mr. Dusen- berry—" There's something worse than that." Mrs. Dusenberry—" What pray 2" Mr. Dusenberry—" To be diMppointed in marriage." HUSBAND—" I've some bad news, my dear; that old bachelor brother of mine has failed lost his entire fortune." Wife—"Oh Jan, bow dreadful! and just as we had named the baby after him. Poor little fellow ! " "You are much taller than you were, a year ago," Aaid a gentlemen to a friend. "Yes, ve reformed; that makes me taller." "And how is tit?" "Well, as I have reformed I have become neees.,,arily more upright." YOUNG WIFE—" Yes, father always gives away etpensive things when he makes presents." Hus- band—" So I discovered when he gave you away!' And then he went to th 6 library to draw a cheque for the milliner's bill.

"DOESN'T your sister float beautifully?" exclaimed Merritt in admiration, as he stood on the beach. " Why shouldn't she," replied little Johimy, "when she pads her bathing-suits with enough cork to make a life-preserver I," CUSTOMER (in restaurant)—" Here, waite two boiled eggs—four minutes, and look lively, I'm in a hurry." - Waiter (hastily dusting off the table-cloth) —" Yes, sah—yes, sah. Have 'ern ready fo' yo' in two minutes, sah, two minutes."

A FATHER, wishing to dissuade his daughter from marrying, said to her, "She who marries does well, but she who remains single does better." "My dear father," she answered, meekly, "I am content with doing well; let her do better who can." 4 HYPOCRITICAL demagogue, in making a political speech, said: "Fellow-citizens, humble as I am, I still remember that I am a fraction of this great Republic," at which one of the crowd exclaimed: "o you are, 'and a vulgar fraction, too 7"

YOUNG HUSBAND (to his wife, petulantly)— "Well, suppose I don't kiss you every morning, on 'taking leave, what does that signify ?" Young Wife (sorrowfully)—" Well, I suppose it signifies that our honeymoon is over." "MR. SAMPSON asked me to be his wife last night, paila." "And what did you say ?" "I told him he must give me a little time, and he said I could have the usual 30 days, or 5 per cent. off for ,cash, and then he steppe and apologised. What am I to think of him, papa ?" "Think of him?" shouted the old man. "That young fellow is full of business, and you can't say • yes' too quick 1" OLD GENTLEMAN (to a very rich old lady at a. party): "Who is that handsome your man stand- ing over there ?" Old lady: "That's my son-in-law. He's- a very brilliant young man—made a large •'fortune by the law." Old Gentleman: " Indeesl I How's that 1" Old Lady: "The law made him py daughter's husband." A SPINSTER friend called on Mrs. Clutterbuck In the afternoon, and over a quiet cup of tea they enjoyed a most interesting conversation on the merits and demerits of a neighbour residing over the way. "How on earth that poor man puts up with it I don't know," observed Mrs. Clutterbuck, "for if you'll believe me, she's out about forty times a day, and she's never out less than an hour at a time." PATRICK--"Moik, dy yez moind roiding this horse to Blinks Corners, foive Moils away, where OM mate yez an' roid him foive miles further, where me brother will meet me and raid him the rest of the way?" Mike—" Sure, Oi'll do that, Patrick, but why do yez be wantin' three men to be takin' one horse fifteen racils ?" Patrick—" It's to make the journey aisy for the horse, ;Wolk." THEY were riding together in the moonlight, and he was trying hard to think of something pleasant to say. All of a sudden she gave a slight shiver.l "Are you cold, Miss Hattie?" he asked, anxiously. "I will put my coat around you, if you like." "Well, yes," she said, shyly, with another little shiver, "I am a Bale, cold, I confess, but you sieedn't put your coat around me; one of the sleeves will do." A STORY is told of Sir James Hannen, who 'presides over the Parnell Commission. He is said to be so correct and conscientious that he has scarcely ever made a mistake; but he did once. A demure, sombre-dressed juryman, in melancholy tones, claimed exemption from serving, and 'his Lordship asked, in kind and sympathetic tones, "On what ground 1" "My Lord," said the appli- cant, "I am, deeply interested in a funeral which takes place to-day, and am most anxious to follow." "Certainly; sir; your plea is a just one." The man departed, and a moment after Sir James Hannen )earned that he was—the undertaker I—N. Y. Evening Post, , ATTLICANT—" I would like a position, sir, in your store." Merchant—" Have you any references, young man 1" Applicant—" No,•sir: but I think I would suit you. I have been carefully raised, and my habits are unexceptionable. I have no vices. I don't know one card from another. I don't know what tea, c.offee, tebaCto, or liquor tastes like. Never go out at night. Never saw the inside of a billiard saloon or tenpin alley." Merchant (dubi- ously)—" I'll take you, young man, but I am afraid I shall not be able to keep you long. You will have a situation as a shining angel before many years— you're too good for such a world as this." IT is related of an impetuous English judge, that, with his usual desire to be expeditious, he once sentenced a convicted murderer to be hanged, and dismissed him without the customary and important closing formula. The clerk reminded him of the omission. " Ah, yes. Quite so," exclaimed the judge. "Bring the prisoner back. Prisoner at the bar, I beg you pardon. May the Lord have mercy on your soul. Remove the prisoner, jailor. Next ease." 5HlO—" I confess, William, that your proposal gives me.pleastge, It would be foolish to pretend that it aoes not, yet--." 11,e —" Yet what 1 What possible objection can you h9.ve to becoming my wife You know that I love you, that laM able to provide for you." " Yes ; but I fear I would be but a sorry 'housewife." "Why so?" "Ilecanse I have never been to a cooking-school." "All the better, dearest; all the better." "All the better?" "Yes. You will stay at home and attend to the cooking, instead of wanting to go out and „ lecture on the culinary art. You are just the kind of wife I want." "Goon gracious, Miss Harriet," exclaimed a young man, slipping hurriedly from the hall into the parlour, "what sort of a man is your father? "About like the average, I guess," she replied coolly; "why do you ask?" "Well he just yelled down- , 3tairs to me to bring him up that poultice for his • sore neck, or he would knock off a piece of my jaw. What do I know about it ?" "Did he see you?" she asked in surprise. "Not that I know 0f.." "That 'mounts for it, then," she said in a tone of relief. IHe heard you moving around, and thought it VMS nether. I thought pa wouldn't be impolite to pests in the house." The young man sat down a, !ew minutes and fervently thanked heaven he was iot the girl's mother.

Private comment has been made on a passage in the reports of the Queen's departure,describing how, when her Majesty embarked, she leaned on the arm of an Indian attendant while the Duke of Conaught walked behind. Her Majesty, who ie faithful in her likes as she is pronounced in her aversions, has put the Indian in the platie occupied by the famous John Brown, who for many years watched over his Sove- reign's safety with a zeal that was religious in its utter devotedness. The Indian successor to John Brown began to take rank about the time of Jubilee. He is a splendid fellow. div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."
Lord Salisbury left town on Tuesday,for Boileaus. His last diplomatic business before the holiday was with the German, French, and Spanish Ambas- sadors, whom he saw at the Foreign Office.
- -After the Queen and Princess Benry of Batten- berg left Windsor for Grasse on Monday, the Empress Frederick and Princess Maigaret of Prussia came to Buckingham Palace, where they are now staying.

A 4riter in "Notes and Queries" has been asking the question who is "the lost leader" of Mr. Browning's famous poem. I thought, it was a matter of common knowledge. I myself remember hearing Mr. Browning say that he supposed the person whom he meant was Wordsworth.

A fortunate farm labourer in Kent has developed some skill in the difficult business of catching stoats alive. He is paid 7s. 6d. for each one by an Australian agent acting for the Government of New South Wales, where rabbits are causing much damage, and stoats are in demand for thinning off the bunnies.

Mr. Orchardson, R.A., will be represented at th e Royal Academy by three portraits. One of these is of Sir A. B. Walker, of Liverpool, whose name is associated with the Walker Art Gallery in that city. In common with many other artists, Mr. Orchard- son has been prevented from finishing his full com- plement of intended work by the dark and dismal weather which has so long prevailed. Thus a large subject picture, intended for the academy, will not be exhibited this season.

Lord Granville, is not yet well enough to leave the town like most ef his colleagues, for an Easter holiday. Sir William Harcourt left for the New Forest on Tuesday; and Lord Spencer is already off to Northamptonshire. Sir George and Lady Trevelyan went to St. Leonards on Thur§day, a day later than Mr. Gladstone, who is the guest there of Mr. Armitstead. Lord Northbrook has gone to Stratton Park. Lord Herschel' has gone to Deal, and Mr. Campbell Bannerman to Paris.

Among the lay readers " ordained " or admitted last week at St. Paul's Cathedral was the Earl of Stamford, whose father died last year at Cape Town. The late earl was a very remote relative of his pre- decessor, the Earl of Stamford and Warrington, but, like him, he belonged to to the historic house of Grey, of Groby, which sprang from Sir Henry Grey, nephew of the Duke of Suffolk, father of Lady Jane Grey, who for a few days enjoyed the empty title of Queen of England.

Although the two champions show so marked an indisposition to engage in the contest at Cork, I am assured that both men are spoiling for a tight. What holds them back is the fear entertained by each one that the other will steal a march on him. They have to resign simultaneously, or there will be no resignation and no contest at all. If the can- test is brought about there will certainly be a Unionist candidate. It is regarded as so good a chance that already several men are enquiring after it.

Miss Mathilde Blind, the well-known authoress, has fled for a time from the fogs and slush of Lon- don to the brighter atmosphere of Paris. There she is revising the proofs of her new volume of poems, which is to be published in the spring season. Miss Blind is also engaged upon a study of Mazzini, which will soon see the light. She knew Mazzini intimately. The great Italian formed a high idea of her literary talent. Miss Blind, by the way, is a strong Home Ruler and an enthusiastic admirer of Mr. Gladstone.

It is not generally known that amongst the offi- cers of the Salvation Army a sort of communism is practised. The Communist motto of "From each according to his ability, to each according to his need "is carried out in this way, that officers are paid according to their needs and not according to their position or the arduousness of their work ; and in some cases the head of a • department who may chancc to be unmarried gets paid less than his subordinates who may chance to be married; the man with a family to .keep getting most, no matter what his position is.

It has just been discovered that the men of the Royal Dockyard at Devonport have been summoned to and from their dihner and other meals for the last sixty or seventY years by the ship's bell of the proud Spaniard's flagship San Joseph. captured:by Lord Nelson at the battle of St. Vincent. The dis- covery was made quite accidentally on some re- pairs being done, and its authenticity is established by the Spanish inscription on the bell, as well as by the dockyards records. The Duke of Edinburgh is stated to have arranged for the transit of the trophy to the forthcoming Naval Exhibition.

We heartily join in the chorus of praise whirl has gone up in honor of the anonymous donor of building for a real National Art Gallery. A. gentle- man who can give away £BO,OOO for the mere love of his fellow-creatures, and with no eye to. his own credit and a possible baronetcy or peerage, deserves the best that can be said of him. But why, oh why, does thin great arid good man make, it a sine qua non that his National Gallery shall. stand at South Kensington? Why not at Whitechapet,Ken- nington, or Camden Town? At any ono oE these places it woad be quite as accessible, and twenty times more" national." Is it too late to remedy this blunder?

I am told that the rider which Lord Berschell added to his judgment in the Sharp V. Wakefield licensing appeal came as a great surprise upon the Lord Chancellor, and that he was not at all satisfied with it ; but it was too late to make his dissatis- faction known. There is no question that the clos- ing words of Lord Herscheltm here he said" he did not think that the fact that a license had been granted for the previous year would be sufficient ground for the justices presuming that a licensed house was then needed and considering only whether the circumstances had changed in the in- terval," were an afterthought. It was noticed that his lordship read the words from a sheet of note- paper, and it is believed they were penned while the Lord Chancellor was making the main deliver- , r ance.

Mr. Secretary Matthews's significant remarks in the Gambling Debate last week about gambling on the Stock Exchange had a dramatic sequel at the dinner table of a popular host the other evening. Conversation turned on the recent enormous deve- lopment of electric lighting. A young buck out of the city. who was of the company, somewhat un- guardedly made the obsPrvation that electric com- panies had been very good business. "For instance," , said he, "I made five thousand in five minutes out of—," and he named one of a fleet of foun- dered companies promoted by a notorious company - monger whose speciality is electrics. A lady who had been listening to the conversation looked up , and quietly remarked, "My husband lost five thou- sand pounds in the same concern, but not with gambling—he was a shareholder." With warmth the city man explained. "I assure you, Mrs.--, you are quite mistaken, it is not gambling at all." "Wardon me," replied the lady sweetly, ".1 am mis- I taken, I remember now that my husband called it swindling and, after hearing the history of thP company, fully agreed with him." The awkward pause that followed was a moment not to be for- gotten.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1891.
LABOUR AND EDUCATION.

would most materially reduce the school rates, and provide, every child with a good education. These endowments, coupled with the immense revenues of the City Corporations, once turned into their right chanr els, would produce such a change as people are little aware of. I can • but hint at the revenues of the church being used for the same purpose. I have so far taken it for granted that the nation as a whole is in favour of Free Education, and, that the trouble now is, how shall the various sects, into which the Christians have managed to divide themselves, be reconciled, and then how shall it all be paid for? One thing I have taken for all that it is worth, and, I think I am justified in this, judging from the correspondent's column of the "Examiner," that we shall have to look outside of the Christians, as a body, to know what Christianity is. Therefore there should be no attempt made to teach it in the day schools. inas- much as the confusion which now exists would only' be worse confounded. As to how it is to be paid for, the means suggested are radical, but they are the steps that could be taken with justice to our old friend the Pious Founder.
BY H. WHITHAM.

Readers of the "Examiner" will not be surprised at my placing the (move heading to anything I may have to say touching education. could not _ _ possibly refer to anything touching the masses, and their betterment, without my mind dweliling upon the labour they perform and the education they have received. It is said, and rightly too, that the masses are not the only workers, that there is a class, not usually included in the term " masses," who work as hard, and as long hours, and who re- ceive far too little consideration. With this class of people! have nothing to do; they are able to look after themselves. At the same time, I may say. that in my opinion, even this particular class needs looking after. Its education has hitherto been upon wrong lines, based upon wrong principles; it has been enabled to learn how to get on in the world, but not how to improve the world. I fancy my readers have no particular desire to read an essay on education, free or otherwise, but having now been in this country over three years, it may be that my views on this question will be accept- able to a few old friends.. What I have to say touch- ing Free Education must be in my own way, because I am quite' sure there are few people who are agreed as to what it is desirable. to do in the way of

EDUCATING, THE MASSES, and what such education is going to bring about in the future. To some people our present so-called civilization'is a complete failure ;yet it is the result of education. The eevelopment of man began be- fore books were thought of, and would have con- tinued if a school-house had never been built. It was in Egypt that education, such as,we know it, or the relative position of teacher and pupil was first recognised, but it was intended to train men only for the special work of the Government. We now claim as a right sombthing very different in- deed. We claim not only the communication and development of right principles,, but the careful, guiding of the intelligence, so that with a perfect educational system our boys and girls shall grow up fully understanding the duties of life. Do we understand the duties of life? The answer must be a sorrowful "No." It follows that the educa- tional systems of the world are failures. And why? In California education is as secular as law can make it. No Sunday laws exist, and, although nearly all the teachers are of the Roman Catholic faith, and ladies, I do not hear tell of any attempt to give religious instruction in the day schools. This may be accounted for by the fact that the Roman Catholic religion here is one of form and‘ce- remony. The people attend church, and in that do all that is required. In the evening balls, theatres, and socials take up the rest of Sunday. It fAllows that during the week the teachers give to their scholars a purely seculat and salfish education. I'do not wish .to be misundersood here ; secular, the education should be. The selfishness comes in irn, perceptibily, because the education implanted in the youthful breast is done intentionally with the view of enabling the pupil to "get on in the world." I can fancy our friends who clamour so loudly for a religious educational system, saying, "Now then here is a confession of weakness from one who has always aefended secularism in our school." Make no "mistake, my friends, I confess -to no weakness. I do not say the religious system failed, but I say sectarianism and bitter cavillings failed, and so were supplanted in England, as here, by something quite as bad, that is, the implanting of knowledge and neglecting the understanding. What does Tennyson say : "Christian love among the Churches look'd the twin of heathen hate."

And so something else was look'd for. Secula/ education has so far failed because it is something like Republicanism in France. It is surrounded by so many traitorous pretenders, each seeking for an • opportunity to undermine it. In the State of Cali- fornia as in the other States of the Union,

EDUCATION IS FREE. ,In the city of San Francisco and wherever need in the rural districts, schools are placed. Each school is made up of various classes, and grades, over which presides a lady or gentleman Principal. The schools are also graded; that is they range from the lowest primary up to the highest of the univer- sities. The scholars are expected to buy their own books; but not being able to do so' *.written state- ment to that effect will procure all that is required. Of course we all know that although education is free it has to be paid for somehow. State appropria- tions of• money are made out of the Land TIOCOS, given by the Federal Government, the proceeds of land either by sale, or, rent, going to the schools. .A Poll Tax is also levied of one dollar per: year on all males over twenty one. By these means a revenue is secured for the support of the schools. How they are t overned, and what they teach is a a long tale, and I do not propose- to touch •upon it. Books giving all this information I will, forward to the curator of the Library, which I hope War- rington will soon be able to call " Free." I have not yet heard of any American statesman, nor yet of any one in this city who would do away with the free educational system which exists throughout America. I find there is a growing feeling towards. making it compulsory. This will be a hard matter. ThezAmericans love, what they are pleased to call theiekliberty.' I am of opinion they don't know,- what liberty is; all the same what little they have of it they wish to retain, no matter where it may. take them to. I have met men in my time who, sneering at the demand for popular education, .asla, "what good will it do?" "Why," say they, answer- gng their own question, "it will only make working: men dissatisfied with their lot, and envious: of otheis." This is quite true, they.nre ." dissatisfied. with their lot." About the envy. I couldn't say, hut given in the sense it is I aim. of opinion that it is. untrue. It is further said, in England, that work-- lug-men wish wish others to pay, for what they ought to pay for themselves, and that it would pauperise the .:people. Two, influential meetings have recently been held in London and one in Manchester on the. I free Education question. The arguments used and reported in the" Christian, World," of January,. 2.9 J, are not such as should) be accepted by Radical Reformers.auless it is on, the half-way princip!s.. I am aware that it was easier to start or take hold of the Free Education principle in America, than it is to do the same thing in England now. America was not burdened with a State Church,no conscience clauses hampered ita. every movement. Voludtary schools wherever they may. made teeir appearance ' were satisfied to do their w.ork and receive their reward. Roman Catholicism, might grin,,but it had to abide by the nation's decree. In England all these "vested interests " are arrayed, against what . I would hope are the wishes of the people.. How 'often has it been said, the history of .Ungland was not taught in the schools I Something going by the name has been taught, but NOT TUB TRUE HISTORY OF ENCII.A.NIN The history of kings and %wens,. of an aris- tocracy and the wars they had brought about,— this has been taught, but not the history of the people's progress,of their yearnings and their efforts, their steady and constitutional efforts to a higher and a better plane, nothing of this has been taught. lEvery Englishman claiming te know anything of ' the history of his country will admit at once that he has gained this knowledge from the daily press, 11 from the literature which is sent broadcast through- 'out the land by the publishing firms. Can it be admitted that working-men would rest satisfied 'with all this talk about pauperising them if they knew the history of all the Guilds of_London and the rich paupers who feast on them ? There are now three-fourtli,s of the children educated at the nation's dxpense. Would the remaining fourth allow things to go on as they are if they knew what the educa- tional endowments of the county were? Why, even' the "Times" has been forced to allow that somo• " Amends is due for the abstraction of immense. educational endowments bequeathed by the wealth y for the use of the poor." I can only give one sam2le,, CHRIST'S HOSPITAL. Stowe tells UB, this school was "established to take poor children out of the street. which was the seed and increase of beggary. and to nourish the ohild.- ren in some good learning and exercise profitable' to the commonweal." To-day this is absolutely alienated from its original purposes. I hove a list before me of 500 children the parents of whom have incomes ranging from 5.300 to £7OO per year. Only 16 out of 500 are the children of the poor:. Each one of the rich parents makes a declaration, that he is a pauper. In the School Board report on endowments, we find it stated that,all these foundations, via., St. Paul's, Charterhouse, Dulwich College, ,Christ's Hos- pital,have practically become midffie.class or upper schools, or are designed to become sounder schemes emanating from the Charity Coromisioners. I have by no means exhausted the list of schools which were originally endowed and intended for the use of the poor. Besides Eton and Harrow there are schools Scattered allover t hgland, which, -were they now used for the purpose originally intended,

And I can give you one other assurance: If I send to England for money, and my letter is faithfully delivered to its destination, the money will be sent to me."

_ "Fear not, my lord; that your letter will fail to 4 promptly .reach the person to whom you write, And now I would like to have you see Sir Richard,. and hear his story. His case troubles me. div.head: LONG, . LONG WALL
div.p: A LONG, . LONG WALL

While the worldia wonderng at Lieutenant Bach- - montoff'a projected journey, mainly on foot, from Vladivostock, on the Pacidc, to Paris, it appears to be forgotten that the proposed feat has already been more than equalled by an English officer. We refer • to Captain Dundas :Cochrane, R.N., whose curious narrative of-pedestrian travel was published in two volumes some. sixty-six years ago. Cochrane's original idea was to demonstrate the -goasibility of walking round the world as nearly as the land sur- - face of the globe -would permit. He actually sue- - ceeded injoyrneying,alome and on footafrom Dieppe. —his starting point—to the remotest north-eastern , corner of. the continent of Asia, the Bay of St. Peter and St. Paul, , Finding it impossible to get a vessel. to convey Mau. thence to the north-west coast,: of America ,he addressed a letter from Okotsk, on , the sea ,of that:, name, to the Governor of ( Siberia stating_ the. reasons which -compelled him, to abandon the further prosecution., of his plans. . He then . set 'out again on foot, and, traversing.. Siberian ,Tartary once more, arri7ed safely in St- Petersburg .jtust three years and three weeks after, - quitting the city 4 where he received a kindly wel- come from,the.Eraperor Alexander-and the British Minister. On one occasion, between. Tosna and Luibane, he was stripped of his valuables by robbersi and tied .to a tree; but he was- discovered and released by some, soldiers who were repairing the road,anki the Governer of Novgorod and a benevolent Russian merchant, provided hira,with a complese • refit. In Kamtschatka he walked four hundred miles , without, seeing a human being, and for one thousand• miles of the-worst' part of his wanderings he met with only one habitation. Wherever people were to be found, however, he was treated with kindness,, and the governors-of towns and:, other Russian ofart cials were, he testifies, ever ready to, help him.for- ward.. .Die details of the systemwhirh enabled him., to brave the hardships and perils, of this stupendous. pedestrian-tour are to be found fully set forth in., Captain Cochrane book.

OTINEH ,BlLLs.—The 'House went into Committee-on the Electoral Disabilities Removal Bill,.and after some dis- cusSion 'progress was reported. Some notices of motion -were given, and the House adjourned until twelve o'clock on Thursday. HOUSE•OF 'LORD,q.—TifIIRSDAY. THE EASTER ADMURTIMENT. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at twelve o'clock. After prayers,•his lordship, with tile 'Earl of Lathom and Lord Windsor, seated themselves on the bench in front of the Throne. All three were in their robes, being Lords Commissioners appointed by her Majesty to sig.: nify her assent to certain bills which have passed both Houses of Parliament. Lord Waldegrave was the only other peer present. The Commons 'having been sum- moned, the Commission was read. The Royal assent was then, with the usual quaint forms, signified to the Tithe Rent Charge Recovery Bill, Consolidated Fund (Nolßill, Seed Potatoes Supply (Ire- land) Act 1890 Amendment Bill, Army ..(Annual) Bill. At ten minutes past the hour Black Rod was announced, and the Speaker, with the before-mentioned members, who by this time bad been joined by Lord Walter Gordon Lennox, proceeded-to the House of Lords to hear the Royal assent given to -various Bills. Upon his return at twenty minntes past twelve, the Speaker intimated that the Royal assent 'had been given to the Consolidated Fund (No. 1) Act and other Acts, and the House immediately adjourned until 'Monday, tho6th of April-

div.head: TERRIBLE DOMESTIC TRAGEIM,
div.p: TERRIBLE DOMESTIC TRAGEIM,
A WIVE KILLING HER HUSBAND TO SAVE HER

LIFE. NEW YORK, TUESDAT.—A telegram from De Kalb, Texas, reports that a terrible domestic tragedy occurred there yesterday. A labourer, on getting up in the morn- ing, told his wife to say her prayers as be intended toitill her as soon as he had put on his shoes. The woman, being thoroughly alarmed by the threat, resolved, in order to save her own life, to take that of her husband. She accordineiy left the cottage, and, proceeding tothe woodstack, secured .an axe. Thus armed, she returned to the house., and split open the man's skull with the weapon while be was engaged in putting on his shoes

THE OPPOSITION TO LORD HARTIN GTON. Maden has expressed his willingness to stand, and it is almost certain his cemdidature will be fully approved by.the council. Oa Thursday night ata largely attended meetiug .of the .ossendale Liberal Council at Rawtenstall, Mr. Jas. Henry Maden, of Rockliffe House, Bacup. /as<enthusias- tically adopted as the -Liberal candidate in opposition to Lord Eartington. Mr. Maelen is about 28, and since his father's death has filled many of the offices Mr. Henry Aladen occupied. He is president of the Rossendale Liberal• Council, and also presalent of the Bacup Liberal Club. !Cr. Maden is extensively engaged in the cotton trade, having three factories at Bacup.

AN UNSUPPORTED CHARGEOF'iTIIEFT.
COLLISION ,BETWEEN MR. P. DIVIES ,AND,
THE CHIEF CONETABLE.

At the Warrington Borough • Police Court, on Monday, Thomas Smallman, a factory hand, resid- ing at 13, Gaghan's-court, was ,charged with steal- ing on or about March let, two cross keys, value 2s. 6d., the property of Ely. Ernest i Lees, manager of the Florence Mills, and Thomas ' Pearson, a carder employed at those mills. Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, appeared for the defence.—Chief Constable Hunt commenced,as usual, to make a statement de- tailing the circumstances of the ,case, when Mr. Davies said he protested against the Chief Con- stable being allowed to make a -statement which might prejudice the prisoner.—Alderman Harrison: You know, Mr. Davies, we do not regard it as evi- dence.—Mr. Davies: But you 'have no right to hear it.—Alderman Harrison: ,I think the Chief 'Con- stable is perfectly justified in .giving,us an outline of the case, in order to familiarise us with the case: —Mr. Davies: But no outline IS ,allowed.—The Deputy Magistrates' Clerk, in ,reply to the Mayor, said the Bench had no absolute right , to insist on having this statement. Mr. ,Davies said Mr. Justice Hawkins had declared that •if any- one except a solicitor made a -statement not evidence, the effect of which might be to pre- judice a prisoner, it was the duty, of, his- solicitor to object, as the magistrates had no right to listen to it. He (Mr. Davies l knew Mr. Hunt was ,an honest. man, and belieted everything he said, but hqw often had his statements turned out quite contrary to the evidence! The reason Justice Hawkins laid down' the principle that he did was that sometimes a prisoner was unde- fended which made these statements against him all the more unfair.—Alderman Sutton did not think Mr. Hunt's statement would be prejudical to the prisoner. Sometimes it was very important that the magistrates should have a preliminary statement+to help- them.—Mr. Davies: But you have to be guided by nothing except evidence.—Alderman Harrison: Certainly not.—Mr. Davies: Then it must be a waste of time to hear Mr. Hunt.—The Chairman said the deputy clerk said the Bench had no legal right to hear Mr. Hunt,. therefore I they ought not to hear him.—The 'Chief Constable: Then am Ito be guided by this decision inluture ?—Mr. Davies: I should submit, Sir, only when objection is made.—The Deputy Magistrates' +Clerk:: 'There is no harm except when it IA objected to.—Alderman Harri- son said Mr. Hunt frequently made remarks to the ad- vantage of the prisoger.—The case was then proceeded with.—Thomas Peathon identified one of the keys pro- duced as his. He did not charge the prisoner with steal- ing the key. The action was not his. Witness was ex- amined as to a man named Whiteley, who, he said,had occasion to use the keys two months-after witness went to the mills. The prisoner had always, as 'far as he knew, been a good honest lad_ Witness further deposed to the prijaner on Friday selling the xey identified, and another at the Marquis of Granby public-house.--Mr. Davies again protest against Mr. Hunt's conduct, complaining that he (Mr. Davies) had asked Sergeant Monaghan a question, and Mr. Hunt had told him to have nothing to do with him. There would 'be an end of his coming to that court if Mr. Hunt was going to be- have like that.—Mr. Hunt said he did not like an officer to be overhauled by a solicitor.—Mr. Davies.: +I should not like to overhaul a man like Monaghan. He would overhaul me.—The Mayor thought Mr. Davies hada right ta ask the question.—Thomas Genty deposed that he bought the keys from the prisoner at the Marquis of Granby.—David Whittaker identified the other key as belonging to the mills —Sergeant Monaghan deposed to apprehending the prisoner who said he found one key and had the other from two Oldham "-chaps*" working at the mills. Witness did not know Whitely came from Oldham.—Alderman Harrison remarked that there was a strong prima facie case, and the chairman thought it was one of • strong suspicion, against some one, whilst Alderman Sutton thought it failed for want of evidence. The Chief Constable admitted that the case was a weak one, but indicated that he would not have proceeded if it had not been for the information supplied him by Mr. London.—The Bench dismissed the case.—Afterseveral other eases had been disnosed of, Mr. Davies, who had left the Court on the dismissal of that against his client, returned into Court and said Mr. London had told him that Mr. Lees had wished to take out a summons and not to have Smallmari locked up, this being contrary to Mr. Hunt's statement.—Mr. Hunt made a statement to the effect that Mr. London had requested that the prisoner should be brought up by the police.—lnspector James made an unsworn statement which practically corroborated Mr. Hunt, though he said Mr. London had asked whether he ought to take out a summons.—Mr. London supported this statement, and said Mr. Lees sent him to the Police Station, and told him that if necessary he must take out a summons.—Detective-Sergeant Monaghan subjected Mr. London to a close examination as to what passed in a conversation between them—The result of this extra- judicial inquiry, during :which no oath was administered, ,was that the Bench exonerated Mr. Hunt, who remarked thatthere was something in the background of it ail, that caused the antagonism against him.—Mr. Davies I object to these slurs; you are not a gentleman. Mr. ' Hunt.—The Chief Constable: You may wait until Doomsday, but -you will have them.—Mr. Davies: You are an impertinent old man.—The Chief Constable: You I have shown the bitterest feeling to me both in public and private.—Mr. Davies: I once beat you at bowls; that is about all.

THE ,CLITHEROE ABDUCTION CASE.
ORDER OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

11.he.order of the House of Lords in the Queen v. Jack son ease was received on Wednesday. It runs as fol- lows :--" Having expressed to the court that in her re- fusal to go to her husband's house, and in her resistance to continue in it, she was acting entirely of her own free will, and had not been forced, compelled, or even in- duced•by.anyone else, it is ordered that Emily Emma Maud Jackson be at liberty to go- wheresoever she pleases."

div.head: WirECK AND LOSS OF 19 LIVES.
div.p: WirECK AND LOSS OF 19 LIVES.

New .YORK, MARCH 22.—The British steamer Strath Airlie, from Santiago de Cuba for Baltimore, has been wrecked of the coast of North Carolina, and of a crew of twenty.six hands, 'nineteen were lost, including all the officers except the,second mate. The Strath Airlie had a cargo of iron ore. It is feared that she will become a total wreck. The Marine ,Court at Gibraltar concluded yesterday the inquiry into the loss of the Utopia. The Court found that the sinking of the vessel and the loss of life were owing to a grave .error of judgment on the part of Captain McKeague. It was not, however, deemed necessary by the. Court to interfere with his certificate.
IMPORTANT LICENSING DECISIONS.

The magistrates of the Tower division of Middlesex,l sitting at Whiteehapel,,have acted with great alacrity on the decision in Sharpe v. Wakefield. In each case of a conviction for betting :they have refused the license and declined to permit a transfer, and in another case they refused a renewal on the ground that the licensee was not the real resident occupier, though he swore that he slept on the premises three or four nights a week. The court was crowded, and the decisions caused so:ne- thing like consternation to AA the trade." On Wednesday, the licensing magistrates for the New- ington aivision of Surrey held their final meeting of the Annual Session at the 'Sessions House. There were a large number of adjournments, of which the Bench refused to renew the following :—The Cross Keys, Savtle-row, Lambeth; Surrey Arms. East Dulwich Canterbury Pilgrims, Lant-st. ; Hop Pole, New Cross- road!, Emigrant, Wyndham-road; Jubilee Stores, Ber- ' mondsey ; and the Green Man, Pricey-st. In reference to the globe, Rotherhithe-at., the police reported that the proprietor had been fined for trading during prohi- bited hours. Within a quarter of a mile radius, there were nine licensed houses and only 311 houses. The Globe was thirty-five yards away from the street, and very difficult to look after.—The Bench refused to grant the license on the ground that the neighbourhood was well supplied, and because the police could not look after it properly owing to its situation. This house, which is close to the steamboat pier, will close on April 5. At the annual meeting of the Glasgow Wine, Spirit, and Beer Trade Association, on Wednesday, Mr. Mc William said he did not think the justices would take advantage of the Sharp V. Wakefield decision.

TERRIBLE TRAIN DISASTER IN AMERICA. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY.—A terrible collision occurred last night on the Chicago and North-west Railway, near Racine, Wisconsin, between a goods train and a pas- senger train. Nearly all the cars were thrown off the line and the wreck caught fire, one sleeping car And several others being destroyed. The stoker of the goods train was killed and thirteen persons injured, two of them fatally. .

The Vicar's version of the affair is that at the time in question there was a choir practice at the church, and, hearing a noise, he went out and saw the assistant and the manager lsaving the school. He told them they had no right to enter the school, and the assistant made what he termed "an impertinent reply." The policeman there- upon asked if he should arrest the assistant, but the Vicar replied that he did not wish to be a party to any- thing of that kind. He saw Mr. Brown and Mr. Gordon coming away " with a great armful of things," and told P.C. Cooper to ask what they had in their possession. Mr. Smith said he had nothing on him, and Mr. Gordon showed the policeman some music books. The men then went away. Mr. Allton denies that he asked the con- stable to arrest Messrs. Smith and Gordon. On Monday morning Mr. Wollacott and Miss Parsons resumed duties at the schools, accompanied by Mr. and 'Mrs. Anton. The proceedings were made the occasion of the gathering of a curious crowd of parishioners and others, who had come in anticipation of a scene. In this, however,they were disappointed, neutrality being appar- ently the order of the day. bat there were sufficient indi- cations to show that the feeling of antagonism between the contending sides had not yet been eradicted. The members of the late staff did not make an appearance, but Mr. and Mrs. Allton, and Messrs. Jenkins and UnSworth, were present. The school bell was rung as usual, and a number of children attended, but many others remained outside, accompanied in some instances by their parents. In the course of about three-quarters of an hour the crowd dispersed, and Mr. Wollaeott and Miss Parsons remained in undisputed possession. Mr. Gordon, while the scholars were assembling was among the spectators in Bostock-st., and there read to the re- porters a written statement which he saia was a descrip- tion of the proeeedings on Saturday evening, in which he gave the version of the vicar's conduct we have already mentioned. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, drove up to the schools in a cab, but seeing that neither he nor his part- ner was required, left the building after a short con- versation with the Vicar.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1891. 'THE ST. BA.RNA.BAS SCHOOL DISPUTE. As was mentioned last week, after the trial at Liverpool Assizes, the St. Barnabas Schools were closed by a notice bearing the signatures of the Vicar (the Rev. G. Allton) and other two managers, against Mr. -Brown, the head-master, and the other teachers, and the scholars were given "a few days' holiday." On Saturdayiafternoon a meeting of the managers, convened by the Vicar, was held at the vicarage, there being present besides Mr. Allton,Mr. oJohn Looker,and Mr. Unsworth,of the firm of Messrs. IJenkins and Unsworth, who acted as solicitors (on belpilf the Teachers' Association)-,'for the plaintiffs, in the recent trial. Mr. Smith, one ot the 'managers, had had notice to be present, but did not attend. The action of the Vicar was confirmed and a resolu- tion was passed, that the schools be re-opened on Monday morning, and Mr. Woollacott be reinstated as head master, and Miss Parsons as head mistress, the Vicar being requested to desire Mr. Alex- ander Brown, who had been acting in place of Mr. Woollacott since the 20th of January, 1890, to give up possession of the keys. It appears that Messrs. 'Jenkitlts and Unsworth for- warded to Mr. Brown the following letter:—" 21st March, 1891. St. Barnabas' Schools. Dear Sir,—We are instructed by the acting manager of the above schools to request that you will attend at the schoolroom this after- noon (Saturday), at 4 30 o'clock, and deliver up the keys of the school now held by you; and at the same time any property belonging to you and now in the said school will bet handed over to you.—Yours truly, JENKINS and UNSWORTH. Mr. Alex. Brown, Lovely-lane."—Mr. BROWN replied that, pending instructions:from his solicitor, he could do nothing in the matter. The vicar, Mr. Looker, and Mr. Unsworth attended at the schools at the time mentioned in the letter, but Mr. Brown was not able to, be present. According to the account ot Mr. Smith, however, he, accompanied by Mr. Brown,and Mr. Gordon, the assistant master, went to the schools., between six and seven o'clock in the evening. Mr. Smith gave Mr. Brown and Mr. Gordon leave to take away any books and documents, and they having done this, the schools were locked up and all three then left. Mr. Gordon dis- covering that he had forgotten some books, went back with Mr. Smith to bring them away. As they wereleav- ing the school, they were seen by the Vical ,who, it is said called out " Police, ' and to P.C. Cooper who happened to be at hand he called out," Search him," referring to Mr. Gordon. The assistant master states that the Vicar asked the officer to "Arrest that young man for trespassing," and said Mr. Smith had no beisiness to enter the school. The policeman said " Will you give him (Gordon) in charge?" but this course was not adopted. Mr. Gordon said he would not allow Mr. Allton to see the documents, but he was willing to show them to the officer, and he did so, and it was found that they bore Mr. Gordon's name. The officer asked the Vicar if he intended to give the men in charge, and the Vicar replied "I would, only ." The officer then asked Mr. Smith where he lived, and that gentleman re- plied "25, Lovely-lane. I shall be there if you want me"

and House of God. I knew in thiS great struggle of life —I felt sure from the first—that we were in the right, yet I never expecced such a splendid victory, and that our enemies would be put tasuch utter confusion. From the first—for my desire is to be, quiet and live at peace with all men—l shrank from publicity. I don'tvrant it, on account of only one thing, and that was our most holy religion of the Church of God, lest in creating a scene we should cause the enemy to blaspheme His holy name. I sat down, as many of you are aware, under every vile thing which was hurled at our Church, my- self, and you, my dear people. I can only thank you for your faithfulness and trust, and the way you have clung round me during the past two years of such affliction. Although this church was never well attended in the morning, in the evening we seldom had a seat at liberty before we were assailed in the manner we have been. Several strangers who came in on Sunday evenings to see for themselves have called upon me afterwards, ex- pressing their surprise to see our congregation, our large choir, our bright and hearty services, as well as the clergy, my brethren, who have preached at various times in this church since I have been here. And now, my dear people, we have had a great trial. It has been a great trial and strain upon me, and upon my health, and it has been a great trial to many of you. Let me ask you, though, to return to your church. Nothing should ever come between you and your religion. Our " light affliction," whiBh has been, as it were, " but for a moment," will pass away, and God will protect his Church and His own. I commend you, then, only to the grace of God and to the power of His grace. Let nit ill- feeling be shown on any account. I ask ytiti only as your minister, to lift up your hearts in thankfulness to God, and to join with me this evening in singinrour glorious " Te Deum Laudamu.l."
CONCERT AT THE WARRINGTON - LIBERAL .CLUB.

On Monday evening a concert was held in the billiard room of the Liberal Club, Bewsey-St.. in aia of the fund for the bazaar proposed to be held in October in connection with the Liberal Association. Councillor Fleming, president of the club, occupied the chair, and there was a large audience, most of the available accommodation being occupied. It was explained that Mrs. Dobson had been mentioned on the placards as one of the artistes, but word had been received from' her after the bills were printed that she could not appear. Mr. Littlewood who was down in the programme for two songs had to be excused from appearing, he having sickness in his family. Part Ist commenced with a performance by a band of which Mr. P. Caldwell was leader, and Mr. E. Whitehead the conductor, consisting of Wagner's March, " Tannhauser," which was admir- ably executed. "The Scout," a song by Mr. James Bate followed, and was deservedly much applauded. Mr. Al!. Cavanagh then came on with a song "Speed on my bark," to which he did ample justice, and received a well-merited encore. Mr. Alf Grounds next appeared in the humorous song "The agricultural show," and treated quite a furore. He was called on to give an encore song, this being also of a comic charter. Miss Cavanagh then sang Cowen's "Chimney corner," in beautiful style, and charmed the audience into giving her an encore also, upon which she sang "Ever faithful," by the same author, in an equally effective manner. Part first was closed with another selection by the band. Part second was opened by the band with a further capital selection after which Mr. A. Cavanagh gave in excellent style" Off to Philadelphia," and receiving an enthusiastic recall responded with a dashing song "A mountebank's life for me." Miss Cavanagh now re-appeared and sang "Sunbeams," by Mrs. Hubi-Newcombe, in a style which, no doubt, would have have commanded for her another encore,had not the Chairman requested the audience not to unduly prolong the concert by recalls. %&r. Whitehead ably took Mr. Grounds place for the next item by singing a rattling humorous song, for which he obtained a well-de- served need of applause. Mr. James Bate then gave in fine style "The death of Nelson," which was followed by Clarke's " Aux Flambeaux,", most excellently played, this closing the programme. Mr. J. B. Caldwell gave much satisfaction as accompanist, and it should also be added that much of the success of the concert, and the credit for the arrangement of the programme, was due to the energetic conductor, Mr. Whitehead. During the evening, Mr. BIRCHALL moved a vote of thanks to those who I had come forward, as he said, to provide the beautiful music the audience had listened to that night. He hoped that this first series of concerts there would not by any 1 means be the last. He was sure they were under many 1 difficulties in the arrangements of that room; and under very awkward circumstances the promoters had suc- ceeded in getting up a very good concert.—Mr. C. J. Hourks, general secretary for the bazaar fund, seconded, endorsine. Mr. Birchall's euloolums upon the concert. He referred to the forthcoming bazaar, assuring the audience that it would be a very grand one. He should no doubt have to ask for a good many things, and he was going to ask for one or two that night. There were some nine or ten stalls to be arranged for, and he was anxious to have as one, what was called a jumble stall, or second-hand stall, a thing which had proved most popular in connection with a previous bazaar in the town. Should there be any members of the club or the Liberal Association who were willing to give subscrip- tions, or goods for the stall, the Committee would be very glad to devote them to that object. He wanted some of them to volunteer for this stall. As most of those present were aware, there was a sewing meeting held in that club, which was largely attended, but he wished to see the attendance increased. He wanted to remove an impression that had got abroad that every lady who attended that meeting was expected to pay ed. a week. Everyone was asked to contribute something, only a penny if she liked, though the maximum amount she might pay was sixpence. There was another matter that would come on later, thedecoration of the hall ; and the committee would require some assistance in that. The proceeds of the bazaar would go to the Warrington Liberal Association, and would, he hoped, put the Asso- ciation into such a position that they would be able to throw such vigour into their work that at the close of the next election they might be able to look back and say that the bazaar had won the election. (Laughter.) If the Liberal Association did not bring out their candi- date very soon, the bazaar committee would find tone for them.--(Applause and laughter.)—The vote was carried with hearty acclamation.—Mr. TnoliAs MORRIS proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, whom,he characterised as in heart and soul and pocket aLiberal, remarking that the concert had pleased him (Mr. Morris) beyond measure. —The vote was accorded, and the Chairman thanked the meeting, though observing that tha credit in connec- tion with the promotion of a concert was due to his friend on the right. The National Anthem was ',played by way of finale to a very pleasurable evening.

div.head: CHILD 'SCALDED TO DEATH.
div.p: A CHILD 'SCALDED TO DEATH.

On Monday afternoon an inquest was held by Mr. Brighouse., coroner, at the Bay Horse Inn Winwick-road, concerning the death of Charles Slater, aged 5 years, son of Charles Slater, labourer' of Manchester, at the house of Mrs. Asson, wife of Edward Asson at 54, Winwick-St. Mrs. Asson deposed that she brought the child to her house from Manchester, on the 14th inst. On the after- noon of the 19th,!she was washing, and about three O'clock left the house for a few minutes to go into a neighbour's leaving a pot of boiling water stand- ing on the floor, and the deceased and her own two children in the room. She had no other place to put the pot. The childin her absence got into the pot of water and was scalded. She called in Dr. Brooks, but the child died about five minutes past four.—Thomas Ireland, labourer, in the Malt Kiln, who lives with Mrs. Asson, his sister, deposed that about ten minutes to four he came home to tea and found the child sitting backwards in the water. Neither it nor the other children were screaming, though the latter were frightened. He took the deceased out and he said he had fallen backwards in. The water was not boiling hot. He called in Mrs. Lightfoot, who applied oil and lime water to the child's body.—The Coroner pressed the witness as to whether the child was not scream- ing, but he adhered to his assertion. —The Coroner remarked, that perhaps the child was then past screaming point.—The witness stated that the water had been off the fire half an hour.— -Mary Lightfoot confirmed Ireland's statement, so far as she was concerned, and said when she took the child's clothes off the skin peeled off.—The jury re- turled a verdict of accidental death.

div.head: ESTIMATES,
div.p: THE ESTIMATES,

The CLERK submitted his estimate of expenditure, and in the course of a statement mentioned that the contri- butions by parishes in the financial year 1889-90 were £18,217, a less sum than in the preceding year. The contributions in 1890-91, the year now closing, were £15,804. There had Wen a fall in the cost of in-main- tenance and out-relief in the Union, as there had been in many other Unions throughout the country. He mentioned that in 1889 the rateable value of the Union was £319,619; in 1890, £323,693; and in 1891, £329,052. —Et was decided to print and circulate amongst the Guardians the Clerk's statement. The relief cases,were then taken.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

It has been resolved by the Irishmen of Jersey City that no invitation shall be extended to Mr. Parnell's envoys to visit that place, and that no money shall be contributed to either section of the Irish party until existing differences have been healed. Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien were on Monday conveyed from Dublin to Cork Gaol. Their arrival at Cork was unexpected, but they were cheered by those of the public who recognized them.

div.head: MR, T. IiEALY BRUTALLY ASSAULTED
div.p: MR, T. IiEALY BRUTALLY ASSAULTED

At the Cork Assizes, on Monday, Mr. Maurice Healey, M.P., obtained a verdict for £5 damages for a libellous statement made by Mr. Roche, a local Parnellite, who stated at a public meeting that Mr. Healey employed bellmen in the towns of Bantry and DunmanWay, for the purpose of obtaining, as a solicitor, the cases of the farmers to the injury of local solicitors. Mr. T. Healy who was engaged in the case on behalf of the plaintiff, on leaving the court, was followed by a crowd of people, several of whom attempted to assault him. On reach- ing hi g hotel, and proceeding to his apartments, he was followed by a man, who struck him a fierce blow across the face, smashing his glasses. Blood flowed freely, and Mr. Healy became quite faint. Three doctors were on Monday night in attendance on the hon. gentleman, and fears are entertained that the sight of one of his eyes may be destroyed. The Cork correspondents of the "National Press "and "Irish Times" state that Mr. Healey has lost five of his front teeth, and is attended by a dentist as well as an oculist.

THE SLIGO ELECTION. Mr. Parnell visited North Sligo on Monday, and ad- dressed a meeting at Ballina on behalf of the candidature of Alderman Dillon. He said the agrarian question in the West of Ireland, and especially in the congested dis- ' tricts of Connaught, still remained almost untouched. It would be robbery and mockery to compensate land- lords for improvements effected by the tenants of small holdings, but he suggested that the Government might spend £8,000,000 or £10,000,000 in redeeming the ten- ants from slavery, the sum being ample fer all land- lords' rights. He condemned the anti-Parnellites for hav- ing deposed the leader whom they had pledged them- selves to serve before taking counsel with tseir consti- tuents on the subject. If there had not been such a frantic hurry on the part of some to obey Mr. Gladstone, a way out of the difficulty might have been found with- out bringing about the present deplorable and terrible Schism.

On Thursday the nomination of candidates for the Parliamentary seat vacant in North Sligo took place, when paperswere handed in on behalf of Mr. Alderman Collery, the candidate of the Irish Parliamentary party, and Mr. Alderman Dillon, the nominee of Mr. Parnell. The anti-Parnellites had a very successful meeting in the Town Hall, Sligo, at which addresses were given by Mr. Sexton, M.P., and Mr...Mauriceyealy,

div.head: MR. PARNELL LOSING GROUND.
div.p: MR. PARNELL LOSING GROUND.

The results of the poor law elections through the country show that the feeling against Mr. Parnell and his supporters is much stronger than even the most sanguine believed. Mr. Thomas Condon, M.P., one of the strongest opponents of Mr. Parnell, has been returned at the head of the poll in Clonmel, while Mr. Luke Hay- den, M.P., an ardent Parnellite, has received a crushing defeat in Roscommon. From Athlone, which was sup- posed to be a Parnellite stronghold ; from Middleton, Cork, and, in fact, from almost everywhere, the reports are equally cheering. MR. PARNELL'S CHALLENGE.

A letter from Mr. M. Healy published on Tuesday, concludes by formally notifying that he has now for- warded to Sir Thomas Esmonde his application for the Chiltern Hundreds, to bm handed in to the Chancellor of the Exchequer concurrently with Mr: Parnell's applica- tion through Colonel Nolan.

div.head: PONSONBY TENANTS
div.p: THE PONSONBY TENANTS
The evicted tenants on the Ponsonby estate have formed themselves into a branch of the Irish National Federation.
THE TIPPERARY RIOT.

The cases of Mr. O'Brien Dalton and four others are charged with riot at the Courthouse, Tipperary, on 25th September last were opened, on Tuesday, at Cork Assizes, and after the evidence of Colonel Caddell and some police evidence had been given were ad- journed until Next day. On Wednesday the hearing was resumed at Cork Assizes before Mr. Justice Monroe. Mr. Power, the sub-sheriff of Tipperary, and several constables were examined for the prosecution, and testi- fied that the crowd behaved in a disorderly fashion. The defendants' case was opened by Mr. Adams, Q.C., who said that undoubtedly there was a riot on the occasion, but it was those who shadd have preserved the peace who were the disturbers. Mr. John Morley deposed to the nature of the attack made on the people. The Courthouse was empty, and the people were refused admission. Outside there was a scene of some excitement and confusion, but nothing that could be termed forcing the gates took place. He saw both Mr. Harrison M.P., and Mr. Keating, one of the defendants, savagely assaulted by the police. On Thursday Mr. Wm. O'Brien, M.P., and Mr. John Dillon, M.P., appeared LS witnesses for the defence. The evidence of these gentlemen, as well as a number of other witnesses, went to show that a disturbance did take place on the 25th September, at the gates Tip- perary Courthouse, but that it was entirely due to the action of some of the constabulary % who first refused ad- mission to the small number of people who sought to go into the building, and then beat them back with their batons. The hearing was further adjournqd.
THE SATURDAY NIGHT PENNY CONCERT AT WARRINGTON.

- On Saturday evening the 23rd and last concert of the season was given in the Buttermarket - St. Wesleyan Mission Room, which was crowded. Mr. John Fairclough presided, and said he well remem- bered the pleasant evening spent with them last season, and had no doubt this would be none the less enjoyable. The programme commenced with a violin solo, a selection from "Martha," by Miss Perry, who subsequently gave "Hope told a flatter- ing tale," .with much taste and skill, and well earned the plaudits she received; Miss Nellie Picton sang "The Better Land," and "A Summer Shower," and her efforts were warmly appreciated; the songs. "Nancy Lee" and "The Lads in ed," were well rendered by Mr. Kerry; Miss Pigot sang "The Span- ish Gipsy" with taste; and Miss Gunton's render- ing of "The Blind Girl to her Hatp," accompanied by Mr. Mather on the harp, was a treat. The same lady was also very happy in her song "Needles and pins." Mr. C. Littlewood's song, " The Children's Home," with flute obligato by Mr. W. H. Podmore, left nothing to be desired. *ln the second part of the programme he sang "The White Squall" with equal skill and feeling. Mr. W. H. Podmore gave a piccolo solo, and was duly rewarded. Miss and Mr. Mather met with a very flatter- ing reception,and their contributions for harp and piano, and a duet„ " Erin-go-Bragh," were musical treats. Miss B. Dutton, of Moore, who has become deservedly popular, contributed a reading " Curfew shall not ring to-night," and an amusing French sketch ; whilst Mr. Furness pro. yoked much laughter by his Lancashire recital " Svyal- lowin' th' boot-jack." Miss Etty Toft accompanied. Refreshments were served during the interval, and a collection was taken on behalf of the infirmary. Mr. S. B. Stringer, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman and all who had taken part in the concerts, said he desired to express, a word of gratitude to all who had tendered help during the seasoii. He could not pretend to mention the names of all, for they were legion, but to omit the mention of a few names would be a sin not easily atoned for. He desired to men- tion the names of the Misses Barlow, Gawkroger, Ash- worth, Vernon, and Lingard, the Secretary (Mr. I. E. Barlow), and last, but not least, Miss Toft, their accom- plished pianoforte accompanist, without whom the con- certs certainly could not have been the source of plea- sure ar.d success they had been. Mr.Nieholson seconded the resolution, which was carried with acclamation. The Chairman briefly responded, and the singing of the Na- tional Anthem brought the most successful concert of the season to a close.

div.head: INFLUENZA IN AMERICA.
div.p: THE INFLUENZA IN AMERICA.
HUNDREDS OF DEATHS.

A Dalziel telegram from Pittsburg says :—" The in- fluenza epidemic is still raging. Seven hundred deaths are reported to have taken place in this city and in Alleghany within the last three weeks, the majority being due to influenza and kindred ailments." The Chicago correspondent of the same agency says :—The epidenale of influenza continues unabated, and is attended by an appalling loss of life. During the fortnight which ended at twelve o'clock last night no fewer than 1,540 deaths have been recorded, or 35 per thousand of the popula- tios.

THE. Sligo contest is having the Mr. rneredParnell effect of demoralising Mr. PARNELL Co. in a more than. ordinary degree. He "went to pieces" during the Kilkenny struggle,. and he is going to, pieces again. Regarding him- self as secure, at any rate, at Cork, he challenged Mr. MAURICE HEALY, who jointly with him repre- sents the constituency, to test the feeling of the electors by a joint resignation. He said—" L am- willing to go to my constituents to-morrow if my colleague in the representation of Cork, will do the same." This statement seemed very bold, and it was, as might he expected, cheered to the echo by Mr. PARNELL'S supporters. It was never: thought that Mr. HEALY,. would have the hardi- hood to pick up the glove; but he had.. He immediately wrote :—" I gladly accept the chal- lenge. Be good enough to let me know the date

upon which you purpose to accept the Chiltern, Hundreds, and I shall ,resign my seat concur— rently, so thht both writs for the city may be. moved for on, the same day." Mr. HBA.DY: added that he wished to come to an issue. without any repetition of the tactics of " Own,- mittee Room 15." And what is the reply ofi the valiant man who was willing to go. before - his constituents .at-,:a day's notice ? He says:— "I have written to Col. NOLAN, the acting Whip

of the (Parnell) Irish Parliameigary party; enclos- ing him my application for the Chiltern Hundreds, and requesting him to forward it to the Chancellor of the Exchever as soon as Mr..MAURICE Thula' has submitted himself to the judgment of anithas gone to his constituents." Was there ever such a specimen of combined craft and cowardice !. In- stead of being willing to resign "to-morrow," if Mr HEALY* -"zwill do the same," he backs out, with the pitiful suggestion that Mr..II,EaLy must first submit himself to tire judgment of his constituents. This brave warrior likes anything better than, close quarters.. In view of such miserable shinning, one is tempted to exclaim with "-Constance" in, "King • John "

Thou wear a lion's hide! doff it for shame, And hang a calf's skin on those recreant limbs. The deposed chief ought to have in mind the proverb about glass houses and throwing stones. He makes his. complaint as to insult on Saturday, and on Monday addresse a crowd at Ardnaree, and. speaks of the majority of the Irish Members.of Parliament (who have cast him off as an unworthy leader). as "forty-five traitors." Is this the language of insult? Or is it to .be accepted as "pretty Fanny's way ?" In the same speech, some of his, late colleagues ' men whose reputati-Ins are unsullied are ' spoken of as the 4‘ black-hearted minority." 11' this is Mr. PARNELL'S idea of politeness, the-' less Ireland has of itthe better it will be for Irsl' land.
