rent year was £31,500,000; but, not satisfied with this advance of £5,000,000, it transpires that there is an additional expenditure of no less than £l,800,000; that is to say, the total estimated ex- penditure upon the army and navy for the current year is really no less than Thirty-eight Millions. And this, too, in a time of peace! Mr. LEFEVRE lays bare the peculiar methods by which this extra- ordinary expenditure was to be provided for, and he adds:—

I have said of these numerous and complicated transactions that they indicate a deliberate policy to withdraw a large mass of expenditure from the cognisance and control of the House of Commons, to reduce the apparent expenditure under the ordi- nary Estimates of the Army and Navy by transfer- ring charges from them to an extraordinary account (a process which no one has condemned more severely in past times than Mr. Goschen), to conceal the real military expenditure for the year, and by a series of shifts and devices, many of them of a novel and dangerous character, to throw the burden of it on future years, and, in their effect, to enable the Chancellor of the Exchequer to claim and deal with a large surplus in his budget, when, if he had paid his way within the year, there would have been a deficit. This is a powerful indictment, and, to the discredit of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, it is proved in every count. After this, we shall perhaps hear less of the " surpluses " of the present Govern- ment. The issue is of importance to the taxpayer, who finds it hard enough to meet the demands of the day without having to look forward to a pile .of debt,:through Mr. GOSCHEN having failed to pay his way in a legitimate manner. When he was at the head of the Admiralty, under Mr. GLADSTON the average naval expenditure was about £9,500,000. For the current year it will, accord- ing to the ordinary and extraordinary estimates, be no less than £19,000,000. The expenditure has more than doubled in a few years; and if John Bull does not mind what he is about it will, like Shel- ley's skylark, go "higher still and higher." Mr. GOSCIIEN is,however, being found out ; he is some- thing of a humbug and a great deal of a failure.
The New THE City Council of Manchester, at Ship Canal a special meeting, has confirmed

the resolution to apply to Par- liament for powers to mihble the Corpora...on to lend three millions of money, on the security of the rates, for the purpose of completing and equip- ping the Ship Canal. It was explained that the ratepayers were so satisfied with the course which the Council were taking, that no poll had been de- manded; and the Mayor added that, if a poll had been taken, the chances were that it would have strengthened their hands, as the evidence from all sides was that the majority in favour of the loan wciuld be overwhelming. As a sequel to the con- firmation of the resolution, the Ship Canal Co. are giving notice of their application to Parliament for a new Bill. The official notice will be found in our advertising columns, and it will be seen that the objects of the measure are" to raise Additional Loan Capital; Extension of Time for completion of the Manchester Ship Canal and Works; Power to Corporation of Manchester to Lend Moneys to the said Company for completion and equipment of Canal Works and for that purpose to borrow additional Moneys; Provisions as to repayment of moneys to and by the Corporation; Suspen- sion or repeal of power of Company to pay interest on Shares out of Capital dur- ing Construction of Works; Incorporation of Acts; Repeal and Amendment of Acts." The House of Commons will need to be accommodat- ing in order that the Bill may pass during the present session ; but there is no room to suppose that the difficulties in the way will be insurmount- able. It is universally recognised that the comple- tion of the canal is a question solely of more money and more time; and it is hardly likely that Par- liament will stand in the way, seeing that the Cor- poration of Manchester, which is amongst the most far-seeing and strongest in the country, is unanim- ous in determining to provide additional capital and accept whatever risk may be thereby incurred. Indeed, taking all the circumstances into account the Legislature would make a mistake if it ran counter to the strong feeling throughout the coun- try in favour of offering reasonable facilities for completing the great undertaking. It is the duty of Parliament to help—not hinder—enterprises which have been well considered by those who promote them, and which are calculated to stimu- late trade locally and improve it generally.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
"Weekly Reader."—We have been unable to trace the quotation from the Act as you give it ; but will inquire further.
It sounds odd to say that the Queen has "gone to Grasse,".and yet it is so.

Good news! It is stated that there will be a reduction in the Poor Rate for Warrington, for the coming year, of no less than 10d. in the pound. But what of the Improvement Rate? Will that be increased ? We shall have to wait a short time for an answer.

Lord Hartington will have a hard fight for his seat. Mr. J. H. Maden, who will be his opponent, is a local man of great influence as a Liberal and a large employer of labour at Bacup. As Lord ilartington is the Alpha and Omega of coercion, it is to be hoped he will be decisively beaten.

It has not been deemed expedient that the Prince of Wales should serve on the Labour Com- mission ; but it is greatly to the credit of his Royal Highness that he should have offered his services. He is willing to work even if he is fond of "play —now and again.

The Cabinet is understood to be a thinking machine, but it is certainly not an acting machine so far as the Commission is concerned. When the Mountain was in labour it d; d at least bring forth a Mouse; but a Tory Cabinet labouring with the Labour Commission has as yet brought forth nothing.

In another column there will be found an in- structive letter from Mr. Whitham—the first of a series of three—on Labour and Education. We regret to learn that he is still suffering from the effects of the rheumatic fever which so completely ' prostrated him last year. He has not been able to do a stroke of work since the first week in Decem- ber; but was arranging to try again the day after writing to us.
The friend who went out with him has been

more fortunate ; he has enjoyed good health, and, getting good wages, has done quite as well as he ex- pected. Mr. Whitham can joke even about his ill-luck., for he remarks in a letter to a friend, that he thinks lie shall turn farmer, as he ".only needs 0 money and experience." It is to be hoped that by this he finds himself very much better, for health is everything to a man in his position.

The decision on the licensing case of Sharpe v. Wakefield has come as "a boon and a blessing to ten." It is the death-knoll of unholy and raven- ous claims for compensation. Already it is being acted upon, for this week certain Middlesex magis- trates have, in several betting cases, refused the license and declined to permit a transfer. This is as it should be. England expects that every Magistrate will in future do his duty.
Mr. Parnell has challenged M. M. Healy to a political fight, and then turned tail. He is like

"Bob Acres" when his valour "oozed as it were out of the palms of his hands." Perhaps he has been reading the reports of the poor-law elections in Ireland, which show that the tide which turned against him in the HOHSO of Commoms is in flood against him in the country. It is beginning to be realised that Parnellism doesn't spell Patriotism.

"At St. Helens, on Tuesday, Elizabeth Tither, who had been 152 times previously convicted, and had been to prison each time, was again com- mitted for fourteen days for being intoxicated." How suggestive this of something. wrong some- where! Elizabeth should be dealt with is a person suffering from chronic disease. Tither should be tethered so that she cannot obtain liquor. It would be better for her, better for the magistrates, and better for the community.

Let bicyclists beware. A member of the wheel- ing fraternity has had to pay 205., at Croydon for personal injury inflicted on a pedestrian who didn't get out of the way—although the bell was rung. The rule of the road is that pedestrians have the first claim to it; and people who go at express speed are held responsible for any ''damage that may be done in a collision. It is a good rule, too, for it has regard to the greatest safety of the greatest number.

The crofters of the far north, who have been turned out of their holdings to make room for deer, are taking the law into their own hands by returning to their ruined crofts. And who does not sympathise with them? Men are of more value than many deer. ,As things go, we shall have meed to alter Goldsmith's famous lines and say : 111 fares the land, to hastening ills a prey, Where deer accumulate and men decay.

A working-man in the North is credited with the following choice flowers of speech :--" There is a little cloud appearing on the horizon, which both parties are playing with as a toy ; yet in that toy is a stinging power which. will before long scorch both parties. That is the labour question, and in it is the stinging germ." In the way of mixed metaphor this is almost equal to the effusion of the orator—an Irishman, wasn't he ? who ex- claimed :—" I smell a rat ; I see it in the air ; let us nip it in the bud."

Sundry cases of adulteration were before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday. The landlord of the Commercial Hotel, at Appleton, was con- victed of supplying whisky too much under proof and 7 per cent. too weak. A milk-dealer of Widnes was found to have sold milk and water, while a provision dealer was brought up for exposing mar- garine for sale without being properly labelled. In each case the fine was one of 10s. and costs only, which was in the nature of a warning rather than a punishment.

John Carney, of St. Helens, will have occasion to remember his visit to Warrington on Saturday. He assaulted an old man, who was walking in the ranks of the Salvation Army,in what was described by the magistrates, after hearing evidence, on Monday, as an unprovoked and cowardly manner. The idea seems to have got into, the heads of cer- tain roughs that the Salvationists are fair subjects for the exercise of their brutality. Carney has been sent to gaol for a month to "cleanse his bosom of this perilous stuff."

It doesn't say much for Oxford University that it should send such a representative to Parliament as Mr. J. G. Talbot. He must have extraordinary ideas of the fitness of things when we find him opposing the opening of national museums and art galleries for certain hours on Sunday, and on the same evening giving notice of motion to reject the bill for closing public houses on Sunday! What would this man of "light and leading" have people infer? That in his opinion it is a virtuous thing to keep public-houses open, but a sin to open a museum? The museum is the place for him—he is a curiosity.

The London correspondent of the "Manchester Examiner " writing on Monday says : The Rev. G. S. Reaney, late of Manchester, preached at St. Luke's, Kentish Town. yesterday morning, the sermon being delivered at a" nigh " celebration. At this church it is the custom to make the communion service and the sermon a sep- arate function. Yesterday being palm Sunday, there was a pr.cessional, the cross being decorated with palms, preceded by four boys carrying palm branches. Mr. Reaney wore a violet stole lined with white silk, arranged over one shoulder, as is the custom for deacons to wear it. In the celebration which followed the sermon, the ritual was not only mtrary to the decisions of the Privy Council, but to the recent judgment of the Archbishop of Canter- bury. Before the communion service was com- menced six tall candles on ..he altar were lighted, the Archbishop only sanctioning two. The elements were elevated, the two acolytes prostrated at the Sanctus, and upon the consecration of the elements the Benedict us was sung before the consecration prayer and the Agnes Dei afterwards. The ablu- tions were performed at the altar, water being poured into the chalice three times, and the cele-1 brant drinking it whilst the hymn, "0 saving vic- tim," was being sung.

.It is amusing to think of Mr. Reaney thus go- ing "the whole hog—bristles and all"—in the mat- ter of Churech ceremonial ; and those of his friends who know his aptitude for seeing the ludicrous side of things cannot but wonder that it does not amuse him too. Lamb said of Coleridge's meta- physcis that it was "only his fun." Can it be that it is only Mr. Reaney's fun to wear a violet stole, and promenade in other man-millinery F But what of this participation in a ritual which is "contrary to the decisions of the Privy Council ?" It really doesn't look well of a convert to become a law-breaker so very, very soon. No objection, however, can be taken to the candles. When a man cannot see his way in broad daylight, he ought to be permitted the use of either six or six- teen candles.

div.head: LIVERPOOL CAB TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE LIVERPOOL CAB TRAGEDY.

PENFOLD'S SENTENCE COMMUTED. The Rev. W. W. Smith, who has been exerting himself in favour of Arthur Penfold, condemned to death at the Liverpool asizes for the murder of Margaret Stewart, received a telegram from an authentic source on Wednesday evening to the effect that the prayer of tha petition, which had been signed during filo past few days and submitted to UN Home Secre- tary, urging that the capital sentence should be commuted, has been granted. It will be remembered that Penfold was convicted of the murder of an " unfor- tunate " while driving through London-road in a cab. The effect of this decision of the Home Secretary, which has no doubt been based upon the plea of insanity set forth in the petition, is that Penfold wUi be detained during the pleasure of the Crown in a criminal lunatic asylum.
WARRINGTON AMATEUR MINSTRELS AT FROD- SHAM.

The Warrington Amateur Minstrel Troupe gave an entertainment in the Frodsham Town Hall, last evening week. It was well patronised, and the audience were kept in a merry vein throughout the evening. After the opening chorus and overture, "Marching through Georgia," songs were in turn rendered by Messrs. E. Gordon, W. E. Hillier, G. H. Yonge, J. S. Haynes, G. H. Houk, and George Rigby. Messrs. Evans and Litton gave the comic duet, "Up to Date." Messrs. Haynes and Gordon distinctly scored in the duet, "It's a good thing McCarthy wasn't there." After the interval Mr. Litton de- livered a stump oration, which was followed by a cornet solo by Mr. W. Bloomfield. Messrs. Haynes and Gordon were very successful in their knock- about act, and the entertainment concluded with a humorous sketch, entitled "The Egyptian Mummy," in which the following took part : Messrs. G. 11. Hoult, F. Worrall, G. 1.1. Yonge, W. E. Hillier, T. Westbrook, R. D. Sinkinson, J. Shaw. Mr. Galloway was the musical director, and Mr. Sinkinson sustained the role of interlocutor with satisfaction. EASTER STIONV OF NOVELTIES.- J. &W W. DUTTON'S, Sankey- st.. Warrington.—Advt. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.
The retiring-Me-Mb-Ws—Messrs. Brown, Siddell, Heyes, Taylor, and Wright, have been nominated, and are re- turned without opposition. CONFIRMATION AT RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.

The Bishop of Chester held a confirmation service at Runcorn Parish Church, on Friday evening, when the candidates were presented from the parishes of All Saints, Holy Trinity, Weston Point, and Halton. His Lordship delivered the usual address on the importance and solemnity of the ceremony. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or hire—GARLAND. Warrington. —Advt.

div.p: RUNCORN BOA.RD OF COMMISSIONERS.

A. special meeting of this Board Was held on Monday night, under the presidency of Mr. W. Fisher. Resolu- tions to draw on the treasurer to pay accounts to close the financial year; to write off the irrecoverable arrears of the general district rate, and to reduce certain assess- ments, were passed. • EASTER SHOW OF NOVELTIES.—J. & W. BuTTos's Sankey- at., Warrington.—Adet. WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.

The weekly meeting of this branch was held on Sunday afternoon, Dr. O'Keefie presiding. Mr. Delaney an- nounced that he had received a cheque for £5 from Mr. Muspratt, J.P.,in aid of the Irish Evicted Tenants' Fund. It was decided to make a more extensive appeal for sub- scriptions. The Secretary was directed to forward £lO as a first instalment from the branch to the joint treasurers of the fund in Dublin.

The last lecture of the series on the political systems ot Europe was delivered on Friday night, when a cordial irte of thanks was accorded the Lecturer, Mr. H. J. McKinder, M.A., on the proposition of Mr. J. W. Light- burn, seconded by Mr. Alfred Harrison. Unfortunately the lectures have been a financial loss,and the Hon. Sec. Mr. E. Wynn Humphreys, informed the meeting that it was proposed to give a performance of Sullivan's "Trial by jury" on the 22nd and 23rd April, with the object :of raising the necessary funds. It is under- stood that Mr. Hudson Shaw will deliver a course of lectures.

With the beginning of the present year, this important examining body adopted a revised system of examina- tions, one of the distinguishing features of which is the formation of Lscal Boards in various districts through- out the United Kingdom, to arrange for, and conduct the various theoretical and practical examinations of the College. A Local Board for Runcorn, Widnes, and the surrounding districts has been formed, and Mr. John Holford, G.P.S.C., of 76, Greenway-road, Runcorn, has been elected as Honorary Local Secretary. In future all examinations in the district,above the intermediate stage. must be held under their supervision. BAssINKTTEs.—J .S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington. —Advt. FATAL AC'CIDIINT AT WIDNES.

On Thursday Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, ore, pd an ingnest upon Hi body of Thoes. Crow' e bond- man, 37 years of age, of 33, Pleasant-street, who died in the Accident Hospital at Widnes, on Wednesday. On the Ist inst. in the course of his duties at the Widnes Alkali Co.'s works, he went to ascertain the quantity of water there was in a tank in the yard. By some means he overbalanced himself and fell into the water which was heated to a temperature of 200 degrees. He walked home, and was attended by Dr. Allen, who at the end of ten days ordered his removal to the hospital so that he might have better attention. Death however took place as stated.—The inquest was adjourned in order that the jury might view the scene of the accident. EASTER SHOW OF NOVELTIES. —J . St. W. DUTTON'S Sankey- st., Warrington.—Advt. 4 ELLESMERE-ST. .DISCUSSION. CLASS RUNCORN.

In celebration of the close of the session, the members of the discussion class in connection with the Ellesmere- st. United Methodist Chapel, held a tea party and con- cert on Friday evening last week. There was a capital attendance. Mr. I. Stubbs; the president, occupied the chair, and opened the proceedings in an appropriate speech. The Rev. J. Martin, the pastor, delivered an ad- dress, remarking that he had never attended a mutual improvement class where the subjects had been so varied and interesting, and the meetings so successful. A most enjoyable programme of songs, &c., was gone through by Miss Heatherington, Miss Cullis, Mr. Weedall and Mr. Leathwood, who each secured an encore. The custom- ary votes of thanks were passed on the motion of Mr. Gandy, seconded by Mr. Scragg. LAWN MOWERS.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington, and at Earlestown.—.Advt.

LECTURE ON MODERN AMUSEMENTS AT RUNCORN. To a large audience in Bethesda Lecture Hall da Mon- day evening, the Rev. Frank Ballard, M.A., B.Sc., author of "Is Amusement Devilish ?" delivered a lecture entitled "Modern Amusements, their use and abuse." Mr. S. Taylor, chairman of the Board of Commissioners, presided. The lecturer in the course of a speech of two hours' duration, spoke of the universal yearning for and necessity of amusement, and said human beings needed recreation as much as food. The forms of recreation might vary, but no man had any right to enter upon them to the injury of labour or in such a manner as to give his neighbours offence. Mr. Ballard strongly con- demned the idea that churches and chapels had nothing to do with amusement: they ought not to be merely places for sermons, prayer meetings, and class meetings. He advocated the provision of amusements of a legiti- mate character, remembering that an amusement that would satisfy @ne nature would not satisfy another.—A vote of thanks closed the proceedings. EASTER SHOW OF NOVELTIES.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey- st., Warrington.—Adrt.

div.head: _ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN,
div.p: _ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN,

With the object of forming a permanent branch of this association in Runcorn, a meeting was held on Tuesday evening in St. John's schoolroom. A large number of those who had received " first aid " certificates were present and Dr. MacDougall was voted to the chair. The balance sheet presented by P.C. Bullock and a statement of the receipts and expenditure at the recent tea party, showed that the branch had a balance in hand of £l6.— The Chairman, in the cours, of aTi earnest speech, urged the members to retain their knowledge. He suggested that officers and a committee should be appointed. Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., was elected president; Superin- tendent Large, hon. treasurer ; Mr. W. Epps, hon. sec., and Committee ; Messrs. Banges, Boyle, Coventry, Clare Henderson, Newton, and the Rev. J. P. Williams, to- gether with Inspector Bowyer, P.S. Woolley, and P.C. Bullock. and P.C. Crowder, representing the police. The ladies' class will probably be commenced in the 2nd week in April. Over 30 ladies have given in their names, and others wishing to join should ,communicate with the secretary.
WIDNES TRADESMEN AND IMPURE
GOODS.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Samuel Hurst, of the Commercial Hotel, Appleton, was summained for selling adulterated whisky. The defendant had sold P.C. Thompson a quart of whisky, which on analysis was found to contain seven per cent. more water than is allowed by law. He was fined 10s. and costs, 21s.—Mary Urquhart, of Lugsdale-road, was summoned for exposing mar- garine for sale without being properly labelled.— P.C. Thompson saw in the defendant's shop a piece of butter labelled "Best mixed Kiel Is. per lb." and be purchased a lb. The county analyst certified that it contained a very large proportion of foreign fat, viz. 75 per cent.. A fine of 10s. and costs, 205., was imposed.—John Irvine, of Dock-st., was charged with selling adulterated milk. The analyst certi- fied that nine per cent of water had been added and a fine of 10s, and costs, 215., was imposed.
It is officially announced that the telegraph office at Iquique has been temporarily c osed by the authorities. The insurgents are reported to have gained another great victory.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATtRDAY, MARCH 28, lB9l. I THE PROPOSED INCORPOAA.- TION OF WIDNES. GOVERNMENT INQUIRY.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATtRDAY, MARCH 28, lB9l. I THE PROPOSED INCORPOAA.- TION OF WIDNES. GOVERNMENT INQUIRY.

On Wednesday, the Hon. T. H. W. Pelham, bar- rister-at-law. the Commissioner appointed by the Lords of H.M.'s Privy Council, held an inquiry at Widnes Town Hall, for the purpose of considering the application and petition of Widnes Local Board for a Charter of Incorporation, according to the provisions of the Municipal Corporations Act, 1882. Mr. Squarey, barrister (instructed by Messrs, Offen- hein and Malkin) appeared on behalf of the Local Board to support the application, and Mr. Howard, rating agent, watched the proceedings on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company; Mr. Barker, for the Sheffield and Midland Rail- way Company; and Mr. Thomas, for the Cheshire Lines Committee. Amongst those present were Mx. F. H. Gossage, J.P., Mr. T. Snape, C.C., Major Wareing, Dr. O'Neeffe, Messrs. D. Wright, S. Sadler, J. H. Hargreaves, J. Christie, G. I. Neil, T. Handley, C. H. Lewin J. Beech, F. Hartland, J. Taylor, J. 11. Lee,4). F. Brookes, J. Chapman, H. B. Shores, J. Midwood, B. Brown, T. Handley, J. T. Allen (clerk), S. Hoyle (assistant clerk), J. Sinclair (surveyor), and 1. Carr (engineer), and many others. The Commissioner opened the proceedings by reading the notice convening the inquiry and the petition of the inhabitants for a Charter of Incorporation. Mr. Squarey said he would clearly and briefly lay a few facts before the Commissioner. In the first place there were 51 occupiers of land in the township, and of these 16 had signed in favour of Incorporation, four had signed against, 19 had declared themselves to be neutral, and 12 were unable to be found. As to house- holders there were 2.131 voters in favour of Incerpora- tion, of whom 125 were females. The total against was 164, of whom nine were females; and there were 696 neutral. There were not accounted for 2,106, that was to say, persons who could not be seen. Alluding to the history of the place, Mr. Squarey said the township ap- peared to have been formerly a rural district, but it had great natural advantages for manufacturing purposes, , the principal one being its situation on the banks of the Mersey, which provided facilities for shipping goods to Liverpool and thence exporting them. There was also a ferry? which had existedfrom very ancient times,crossing the river from the Lancashire to the Cheshire side, and vice versa. Another advanistV was the proximity of the district to the coalfields St. Helens. The Sankey Canal connected St. Helens and Widnes, and afforded great facilities for obtaining the coal- necessary to carry on the large works which now existed. There were three railway systems running through the place, the London and North. Western, the Sheffield and Midland, and the Cheshire Lines. The first railway was authorised in 1830, from St. Helens to Runcorn Gap. The Commission would at once see there was every opportunity in Wid- nes for carrying on a large trade indeed. Previously to 1846. the Sankey Canal and certain railways had been amalgamated and certain farsighted gentlemen saw then was the time to inaugurate works and start Widnes. Ac- cordingly about that year alkali works were started by three gentlemen whose names were well known in the country—Mr. Wm. Gossage, Mr. John Hutchinson, and Mr. McClellan. From this small beginning 40 years ago the town of Widnes had arisen. The works of Widnes had increased to an enarmousextent,trade had increased proportionately. Originally in 1846 there was only one alkali works, now there were fourteen, three copper works, three foundries, one large soap works, one manure works, and a number of smaller works. The area of the present township was 3,039 acres, made up of 1,489 acres of quasi agricultural land, 160 acres of railways, docks and canals, and 1,490 acres of houses, works, streets, &c. Widnes was at one time part of the ancient parish of Prescot, and it was now divided into three ecclesiastical parishes of Fern- worth, St. Ambrose, and St. Mary's. The present bound- aries were on three sides bounded by rural sanitary townships, and on the south side by the river Mersey. With regard to population in 1851 there were 3,217 in- habitants ; in 1888 when a special census was taken, the population was 29,723 and it was now estimated at 30,612. The number of inhabited houses in 1871 was 2,517 and in 1890 the total numinr of houses was 5 ,166 ; and the number in course. of erection in March this year was 70. The Surveyor would tell him that the de- mand for houses was considerable. In 1880 the number of building plans passed by the Local Board was 57; in 1890, 112, a very large increase. In 1867 the gross value of the township was £37,625; rateable £31,846, assessable, £26;755. In 1889-90, the gross value was £184,405, rateable £139,339, assessable, £114,449. The total expenditure on general district rate in 1890 was £13,079. Widnes gave its 'name to a Parliamentary division of which it was the centre, and one member was returned. A few years ago when the County Council was constituted, Widnes was given one member and now the claims of the town to representation had been recog- nised by giving the township another member. With regard to Poor Law administration Widnes was in the Prescot Union,•and originally had two representatives; in 1881, the Guardians were increased to three, and since 1883 there had been four Guardians. The poor rate was Es. iu the .C, ane in 1890 ,the total charge was .00,325. relief commitee attended at Widnes weekly. In regard to educational statistics, there was a School Board, which was established in 1874 and was composed of 11 mem- bers. The total school accommodation provided for 6,992 children. There were three Board Schools which had accommodation fcr 3,381 children' with an average attendance of 2,815. Five denominational schools had accommodation for 3,381 children and an average attend- ance of 2,646. The cost of the sites and buildings of the Board Schools was £36,585. There was also Farnw oral Grammar School, on the governing body of which the Local Board was represented by two members. Widnes Science and Art School, with an accommodation for 100 pupils, was in a flourishing state; and was managed by the Local Board under the Technical Instruction Act, 1889. Briefly, the Local Board was constituted in 1865 and con- sisted of 9 members ; in 1875 the number of members was increased to 15/At which figure it remained. There had been nodivision into wards. The Board owned two very important properties in the gas and the water works. The gas works were purchased in 1867 at the arbitration price of £8,669; and there had since been expended on capital account the sum of £67,566. In every year the works had yielded a profit until 1889 and 1890, when there was a small loss accounted for by the fact that great alterations were made in the works, which would have their effect in futureyears. With regard to water supply, itwas unsatisfactory in 1867, and the Board very wisely purchased them at the arbitration price of £8,669, and there had, up to the present time, been expended upon them on capital account the sum of £230,700. The water was sold at a very cheap rate, and the profit on the works was very considerable, amounting in 1890 to £1,610. Mr. Squarey described the area through which gas and water was distributed and the great extent and value of the works. There were very large public baths in the town provided by the liberality of a local gentle- man. The property belonging to the Local Board was as follows ;—Gas Works, Water Works, Accidental Hospital, Infectious Diseases Hospital, Market building and land, stables and store yard, Town Hall, offices and library, house and garden,Appleton ; West Bank Promen- ade, open space Warrington-road, fire station and cottages in course of construction. The expenditure by the Local Board on permanent works amounted to £347,999 and there was a further expenditure proposed on fire engine station and cottages, £3,000; altera- tion of public road, flagging, 14c., in public road, £2,086; private streets £7,697, the latter of which. would be repaid in time by the property owners.' With respect to the local rates, they had varied i from 3s. 4d. in 1871 to 4s. 10d. n 1881 and 4s. 6d. in 1890, when they were made up of poor rate 25., general district rate 2s. 6d. There was an effi- cient sewerage system, discharging into the river Mer- sey, the lengtii of the public sewers being 12 miles and three-quarters. There were 33 miles of streets and 10 miles of passages. Alluding to the administration of justice, it was pointed out that Widnes was in the petty sessional division of Prescot, and a court was held each Thursday and more often if required. Two justices resided in Widnes, six were in Widnes almost daily, being owners of works, and the magistrates' clerk or his deputy is in daily attendance. The number of police were as follows: 1 superintendent, 1 inspector, 5 ser- geants, and 29 constables. The police service was very efficient. A county court was held monthly.—Mr. Squarey in conclusion said the desire for incorporation had arisen on numerous occasions in past years and it took practical shape in August, 1890, when the Local Board were petitioned to apply for a charter; a canvass of the ratepayers Was made and there being an over- whelming majority, in favour of such a course, an ap- plication for a charter was made. The reasons • given for this application were, first the perhaps senti- mental reason, but one which was bound to have con- siderable weight, the' desire to be more independent in governing their own town,and there was no question— one saw it every day—that the position of a corporation in public matters was considerably better than that of a Local Board. This was seen especially in Parliamentary matters. A petition from a Local Board had not so much weight attached to it as a petition from a Corpor- ation. Then as to borrowing powers, it was hoped, and the hope was based on reasonable expectations, that money could be obtained at lower rates of interest than at present; which would be a benefit to the township. In course of time the town could have its own borough bench, and have control of its own police. Then there was the important fact that in a corporation the rate- payers would have a larger choice of people to represent them. The present qualification for a member of a Local Board was £3O rating or the possession of property value £l,OOO. It might not be a large qualification, but it had kept away many gentlemen well fitted to carry out duties of local government. Then, a member of a Local Board must reside within seven miles of the town- ship, and many whom that restriction had prevented from serving the ratepayers would be eligible to act on a Corporation when the distance was much extended. Amongst other advantages of incorporation would be the immense improvement in the voting machinery. At present members were elected by voting paper, and if there was a corporation it wouldbe by ballot, which was immesurably superior. Then there would be one man

one vote, which was rightly considered a very great ad- vantage. It was proposed to divide the township into six wards as follows : No. of houses Rateable Ward. Population. Acreage. & burgesses. value. Farnworth 3,306 ... 1.150 ... 551 ... £11,043 Halton ' 4,644 ... 677 ... 774 ... £33.138 Simms Cross. 5,742 ... 247 ... 957 ... £11,417 Victoria Waterloo 6,060 ... 402 ... r,-oio ... £31,404 West Bank 4,854 ... 296 ... 809 ... £30,667 The first witness called was •

./sfr. F. H. Gossage, who said he was a county magis- trate and Chairman of the Local Board. He was a mem- ber of the firm of W. Gossage and Sons soap manufac- turers, who employed 670 persons, and their weekly wages bill, exclusive of salaries in office, was about £BOO a week. The rateable value of the works was £2,834. He had been a member of the Local Board since 1869 ; Chairman since 1882, and Chairman of the Gas and Water Committee prior to that time. In4o years the population of the town had increased ten times, and in 30 years the rateable value had increased three times over. Widnes was the centre of the alkali trade, and there were capital facilities for trade. He considered great advantages to the town would follow incorpora- tion. It would be a distinct advantage to have the Mayor and ex-Mayor sitting on the Bench with the county jus- tices. He confirmed parts of the barrister's speech.—Mr. Thomas complained that his Company had not received notice re the proposed incorporation until the 9th March. —The Commissioners said they were not obliged to have notice at all. The Company had property in the town, and they must look after their own interests, and now was the time. (Laughter).—Mr. Squarey, said the Sheffield and Midland Railway had their own representa- fives on the Board. Mr. Thomas Snape, C.C., chairman of the County Technical Education Committee, said he had known Wid- nes since 1856. He owned a manufactory which was rated at £492, and also owned other property in the township. In his opinion Widnes by its size and import- ance was entitled to become a borough. He endorsed the statements made as to the advantages that would accrue. He lived outside the seven miles limit and if the town were incorporated he should be eligible for a seat on the Council. Mr. J. T. Allen, clerk and aocountant, described how the canvass was taken, and verified the figures given by counsel.—Mr. Howard : It is not suggested that Wid- nes is badly manaked by the Local Board ?—Not that I am aware ot.—Mr. Howard: It is efficient. You can- not improve on that.—Yes, you can have it more effi- cient. (Hear, hear.) Mr. H. IVade Deacon, J.P., who was absent through illness, wrote supporting the application for a charter. Major Wareing said he was an oil merchant and grease manufacturer. He was Chairman of the Hoard of Guar- dians of the Prescot Union, a member of the Widnes School Board, and Chairman of the Finance Committee. He was intimately acquainted with the people of Wid- nes, and there was a strong feeling in favour of incor- poration. The present system of voting for members of the Local Board was very clumsy and unsatisfactory,and this would be done away with on incorporation. He mentioned other advantages. Mr. J. S. Sinclair, surveyor, corroborated the state- ment made by counsel as to sewers, streets, and house property.—Mr. Howard argued that a portion of West Bank Ward and a portion of Halton Ward 11 should be struck out of the boundary, there being I practically no houses and only a few works there.—The Commissioner said in making a borough or an urban district it was most important that .all buildings should be under the government of the borough, and he hoped before long local authorities would exercise a strong power over works of.this sort as regarded the emission of smoke and other things. (Hear, hear, and applause.)—Mr. Thomas wished Farnworth Ward to be excised from the scheme, because it was principally agricultural land, but the surveyor said that was becoming the residental portion of the township. Mr. I. Carr, gas and water engineer, said there were 30 miles of gas mains and 50 miles of water main, and the whole district and villages outside were supplied. The amount of water supplied was rapidly on the in- crease. In 1890 790.250,000 gallons were supplied, but during the year ended that day close on 1,000,000,000 gallons had been supplied. At this point the Commissioner entered into a conver- sation with the railway representatives to shbw that the companies would benefit little by their lines running through rural instead of urban districts, because they would find in a small borough that the rate did not in- crease above 2d.—Mr. Howard: I think 2d. is a most moderate amount—if we could get such a guarantee as that.—The Commissioner: There is no guarantee. (Laughter.)—Mr. Howard: There is no limit to the borough rate, and we generally find that Co•perations when established do not forget to spend money.—The Commissioner replied that the borough rate included the school rate and the sanitary rate, which were levied ex- actly as under a Local Board.—Mr. Howard: We have certain privileges under the general district rate; if this charter is granted a large proportion of the expenses which is now met by the General District Rate, will come under the borough rate.—The Commissioner: I say a small proportion indeed.—Mr. Howard: Suppose they enlarge the Town Hall, which is contemplated, the addi- tional exOnse will come under the borough rate.—The Commissioner: It is possible that might be charged in the borough rate.—Mr. Squarey: We have powers already to borrow R• 25.000 for the construction of the Town Hall.— Mr. Howard: That is a very important item indeed. ' Dr. O'Keefe said he had practised in Widnes sines 1865 as a physician and surgeon. The feeling of the popula- tion was almost unanimous in favour of inc -irporation.— The Commissioner: Is Widnes an exceptionally healthy place? (Laughter.)—Dr. O'Keefe: Our rate of mor- tality is really very good considering the appearance of the town. —The Commissioner said he was told in Man- chester on the previous day that the mortality of Wid- nes was low because the doctors wGuld not allow anyone who was ill to remain there. (Laughter.)—Dr. O'Ke2fe said the town had two excellent institutions in the In- fectious Diseases Hospital, and the Accident Hospital, which were of great advantage. The rate of mortality was not more than 19 per I,ooo', which was very low for a place like Widnes.—The Commissioner: It is.—The Commissioner then invited the representatives of the railway companies to speak, and Mr. Howard said the matter was a most important one indeed to railway com- panies, who derived not the least benefit frim municipal government. They contended that under the old state of things they had ample powers for properly adminis- tering the district; and they hoped that if he did not see his way to refuse the application entirely, he would at least make some modification which would exclude the agricultural portion of the township, or if that could not be done, they would be satisfied if the new corpora- tion would give them. differential rating such as they had at present under the Local Board.—The other rail- way representatives concurred, and the rateable value, of the companies were stated as follows :—London and North - Western, £19,932; Cheshire Lines, £1,623 ' • and Sheffield and Midland, £l,lOO. The Commissioners said it was very natural that railway companies should be represented on such occasions, bat the Municipal Corporations Act did not direct that any attention should be paid to the wishes of railways or the owners of land ; it was a matter for the inhabitant householders and he could not hold out any ' hope that the opposition of the railway companies would I have much effect as regarded the granting of the Charter. , As to the question of differential rating there was no power either by charter or scheme to alter the principle lon which the rates were levied. With regard to the I suggested alteration of the boundaries, the agricultural parts were already included in the township, gas and water was laid throughout the entire district, and the owners of property in the agricultural parts had not joined the opposition. He did not wish to give a decided opinion as to the granting of the charter; that was a I question entirely for the Privy Council; but the ques- tion of boundary was left to his discretion, and he felt that the omission of any part of that would give a good deal of discontent not only to the people of Widnes, who might regret losing part of their area, but he thought it would not be regarded with satisfaction by the inhabit- ants' of Farnworth itself. The Commissioner then read a letter from Mr. Hulton, clerk to the Lancashire County I Council stating the Council did not propose to offer any I opposition to the proposed incorporation of Widnes, in- asmuch as they were of opinion that whenever a local authority desired to change its form of government it was not part of the duty of the County Council to stand in the way, providing the rights of the county ratepayers were protected.—Mr. Squarey on behalf of the Local Board thanked the Commissioner for the extremely courteous way in which he had conducted the inquiry.— The railway representatives joined in that expression.— The Commissioner suitably replied.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at the Work- house, Dutton, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton pre- sided, and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Baguley, Lewis, Heywood, W. Whitlow, Pickering, Weir, P. Hall, Parr, J. Bate, E. Aaron, J. W. Kirkham, Mountfield, C. Philips, J. Knowles, J. Mclntyre, Bretherton, H. G. Linaker (clerk.) THE POLLUTION OF KECKWIDIE BROOK. The Clerk said he had as instructed, written to the Local Government Board asking for particulars of the scheme submitted by Mr. Earp, and the Board had replied that the application would receive their attention. THE NOXIOUS GASES AT WIDNES. The Clerk said he had received the following letter from the United Alkali Company :—ln reply to yours of the 12th inst., calling my attention to alleged escapes of acid gases from works at Widnes. I beg to say that all the works included in the Company, are witn the exception of two, Alkali Works and as such are under the very stringent regulations of the Alkali Acts, which insist, as you are aware, upon the condensation of acid gases, and constant inspection by Government inspectors, who are appointed for this purpose under the provisions of these said Acts. The two works which I have named as ex- ceptions do not manufacture either vitriol or hydro- chloric acid. I also beg to point out that there are other works in and near Widnes which involve acid gases largely, and which are not under the provisions of the Alkali Acts, and are not under Government in-

spection. I may also add that the directors of the United Alkali Company are extremely anxious not only to prevent the escape of acid gases, but to pre- vent the escape of disagreeable gases which though they do not injure may cause annoyance ; with this object the directors have recently appointed two special inspectors of practical expel ience whose duty it is to visit the works at all hours of the day and night and to report upon any deficiency they may find in man- agers, workmen, or plant. This, I think, will show you that the directors are in earnest in this matter. I beg to remind you that some injury to vegetation must ensue on neighbourhoods where enormous quantities of fuel are burnt on a limited area. This is seen in the vicinity of all manufacturing towns, and is caused by sulphurous acid, which is produced from sulphur in the coal and for this all consumers of coal are alike responsible.— Yours truly, EusTAcE CAREY.-Mr. Aaron said he knew the Company had two men for day and two for night to visit the works at all hours, and they did not report to- the manager or foreman of the works, but direct to Mr. Carey,and if there were any escapes of gas the managers were in hot water. He believed everything possible was being done.—Mr., ravr said since he last made his com- plaint, it had Dot been like living in the same country. He had never smelt a bit of noxious vapour.—Mr. Hey- wood: Has the wind been in the same direction.—Mr. Whitlow It has been in the east during the last fort- night.—Mr. Heywood : I think the wind has had most to do with the alteration.—Mr. Aaron: I think it is going to be better.—The Chairman: We can't take the matter any further.
SCARLET FEVER. The Medical Officer (Dr. Adams), reported the outbreak of two cases of scarlet fever at Frodsham. Both cases were very mild, in fact no " peeling " had taken place so far.
RUNCORN CRICKET CLUB.

The members held their annual dinner at Wil- son's Hotel, 141 t evening week, the catering of Mr. and Mrs. Cooper being highly satisfactory. There was a good company present, and Mr. S. Taylor. the president, occupied the post of honour. lie was supported on his right by Mr. J. R. Frith and on the left by Mr. Superintendent Large. On the cloth being drawn the Chairman submitted the usual loyal toasts. Mr. Frith proposed "Success to Runcorn Cricket Club" in a neat speech, remarking that he had taken an interest in the game all his life, and he was the oldest cricketer present. He had been connected with cricket in Runcorn since 1864, but as age crept on he had had to cease from playing, although his heart was quite as much in the game as ever, and he trusted the coming year would be a most prosperous one for the club. (Applause.) Some (rood matches had been ar- ranged, and they had not had a better card of fixtures for several years past. Everything looked hopeful for a successful season. (Applause.) The toast, with which was coupled the name of Mr. Henry Wright, the captain, was enthusiastically drunk.—ln respond- ing, Mr. Wright said matches had ben arrangel with Clubman.' Widnes, Pearson and Knowles, Warrington 2nd, Stanley, Chester, Garston, Sze., and the club had a good prospect for the season. They had a good ground, they expected to have some new blood introduced into the club, and if the members would rally round the officers, they would have a victorious and successful season. (Applause.)—Mr. J. J. W. Potter proposed "The President" in terms of eulogy, and the toast was drunk with musical honours.—ln reply the President expressed his pleasure at being present. He said he had never played cricket, and his only object in accepting the position of president was to promote and help forward in every way the cause of healthy recrea- tion, because he thought that in the past Runcorn had been short in this respect. He was a great believer in recreation, especially at the end of a week of laborious work, because he beliefed it was beneficial in every respect. The Saturday half - holiday had been a great blessing to the working popu- lation of the country— (applause) —it had given an afternoon for recreation which had prepared them to resume their duties on the Monday morning, and as for Runcorn Cricket Club, he did not see why they should not have a club equal to any in the country. (Applause.) As president he should be pleased to help it all he could. (Applause.)—Mr. James Frith proposed" The officers of the club," coupling with the toast the names of Igr. Jesse Thnmins, treasurer ; Mr. George Frith, the *re- tary ; and Mr. H. Wright, captain, and each of these gentlemen responded. The Chairman then gave "The town and trade of Runcorn," and said he felt sure that Runcorn had a future before it. The Ship Canal passing so near to the town and the numerous works that bad arisen and were likely to rise, pointed to the fact that there was no town within many miles that had a better prospect of prosperity than Runcorn. No town between Eastham and Manchester would derive more benefit from the Ship Canal than Runcorn. (Applause.) Mr. Potter responded, and expressed concurrence in the President's sentiments.—Other toasts followed including the health of Mr. Frith, The Press, and the Host and Hostess.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at the Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. J. Baguley, Lewis, Hey- wood, W. Whitlow, Pickering, Weir, P, Hall, Parr, J. Bate, E. Aaron, S. Taylor, J. W. Kiraam. Moun- field, C. Phillips, J. Knowles, J. Mclntyre, Brether- ton, Fisher, J. W. Baguley, Jackson, and John Whit- low.
VOTE OF CONDOLENCE.

The Chairman said before the business commenced, he had a motion to propose which he was sure they would all agree to. Mr. Linaker, who died last week,had been Clerk to the Board 27 years,and during the whole of that time, he had most zealously and efficiently discharged the duties of the office. He thought no one could say he had ever made a mistake, and he had been a guide to the Board in all their work. He therefore moved "That this meeting regards with deep sorrow the death of Mr. Henry Linaker, who for 2? years was Clerk to the Board, and most zealously and efficiently discharged the duties of the office, and desires to express the deepest sympathy with Mrs. Linaker and the members of the family in their bereavement."—Mr. Mclntyre said many of them had not only lost an efficient officer, but a dear friend by the death of Mr. Linaker, and he seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.
THE VACANT CLERKSHIP.

A letter was read from the Registrar General, directing the Board to appoint a succesor to the late Mr. Henry Linaker, superintendent registrar for Runcorn Union.— The Chairman said he had written to the Registrar General with regard to postponing the appointment until the next meeting of the Board and he had received a reply that he would give effect to their nomination on that date.—Mr. Mclntyre moved and Mr. Fisher seconded,that the appointment be deferred until the next meeting.— Carried.—The Chairman said there were two courses the Board could adopt in appointing a clerk to the Board— either notice must be criven of the meeting at a meeting previous,or they must advertise. In his opinion it would be best to advertise as they had done in other appoint- ments; and also if a Committee were appointed to con- sider what the emoluments of the clerkship were.—Dr. Gastaldi proposed a resolution to that effect.—Mr. Hey- wood seconded.—Mr. Aaron considered it was unneces- sary to advertise, which with the railway fares of applicants, would amount to £lo.—Mr. Fisher said do not let them go into this cheese-paring ; let them make the appointment in the usual way.—Mr. Parr said adver- tising was throwing money away. They had got first and second present—(laughter)—he would bet that. (Laughter.)—Mr. Fisher : Mr. Parr is in the secrets.— Mr. W. Mclntyres said Mr. Parr had no right to assume anything of the sort, and he thought it would be better to make the appointment without any suspicion of hole and corner work.—Mr. Parr: I think there is great suspicion of wasting folks money. (Laughter.)—Mr. Heywood: Somebodymay apply who will do the job for nothing. (Laughter.)—The Chairman said the salary of the clerk was £9O. The Assistant Clerk: £80; there is £lO for the assistant clerk which was sanctioned by the Local Government Board.—The Chair- man said they would find that the assistant clerkship was not a permanent appointment.—The Assistant Clerk asked, should he place in the advertisement, in all probability the clerk would be appointed to other offices, ' and a long discussion ensued; eventually it was decided to advertise for a clerk at £9O and men ion nothing about other appointments.—The Assistant Clerk said at Preston the Clerk to the Guardians to the Rural Sanitary. Assess- ment Committee, the School Attendance Committee, &c., were all separate appointment.—Mr. Fisher: Surely such a sweeping change as that is not contemplated here. (No, no.) The following gentlemen were constituted a Committee to consider the various emoluments of the clerk and consider the application previous to the next meeting :—Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Hes-wood, Brandreth, Taylor. Fisher, W. Whitlow, Knowles, Mclntyre, John Weir, Lewis, and P.lll.

div.head: ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE..
div.p: THE ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE..

The Assessment Committee r:e-P-c-ii-ted that they had considered the remuneration of the clerk for the past year, and a statement of the work done being submitted, it was unanimously resolved that for the ordinary duties in connection with the Committee, the late. clerk be paid the same amount as last year, viz.,£Bs ; and it was also resolved unanimously that in consideration of the addi- tional labour imposed upon the late clerk during the year in connection with the inspection of the accounts of the River Weaver Trustees, from 1884 to 1889, and there-arrangement of the Assessments thereof, inspecting the works of the salt union in the township of Weston, the Britannia Telegraph Works in the township of Helsby, and increasing the assessment thereof, °ringing into assessment a new dock and smithy, in the township of Dutton, belonging to. the Trent and Mersey Naviga- tion Company, re-arrangmz the assessment of tithes in the townshiPS of Kingsley, Helsby, Frodsham, Frodsham Lordship, Manley, Newton by Daresbury, Alvanley and Norley, and for extra work in the appeal against the assessment of the Appleton Quarry, a further amount of £55 be paid to the late clerk for such extra services; and that the sanction of the Local Government Board be obtained to the payment of both sums,—The report was adopted on the motion3oftMr, W. div.p: RE-APPOINTMENTS.

div.head: TRANSFERENCE
div.p: A TRANSFERENCE

Dr. Gastaldi said there was only 8 people in the House belonging to his religious denomination, and one of thes‘ was a little boy, and he proposed that he be sent to the Stockport Institution where he would be educated, taught a trade and made a useful member of Society. The charge would be 4s. per week and the cost of keep- ing him in the House was 3s. 6d. The girls who were sent to Pantasaph were doing very well.—Mr. Kirkham seconded the motion which was carried. ONLY A PAUPER "RATTLE HIS BONES" &C.

Mr. Mclntyre said there were very serious rumours ghat with respect to the manner in which a pauper named Rustage was buried at Little Leigh church. The grave was found too short for the coffin, and it was stated that the man in charge danced on the top of the coffin and by that means got it into its place. The second charge was that the body was not taken into the church, and the third was that, after the funeral, the grave was left unfilled, waiting until such time as there was another pauper ready.—The Chairman: For some days.—Mr. Mclntyre: Yes, for some days.—Mr. Jack- son said at Little Leigh paupers graves were not pro- perly covered over until filled with coffins. The coffin was covered with a little sand and planks.—Mr. Taylor: What thickness of sand.—Mr. Jackson said he did not know, but the coffin could not be seen. As to not tak- ing the coffin into the church, the place was undergoing repair, and the heating apparatus was out of order, and no coffin whatever, had been taken into the church for a long time past. He knew nothing about the dancing.— The Assistant Clerk said the Board paid 13s. 4d. for a new grave, and 6s. 2d. for re-opening a grave.—Mr. Heywood whose duty is it to see the interment properly carried out.—The Clerk: The sexton.—Mr. Mclntyre: I don't think it is well to have distinctions in regard to paupers.—Several members :—No, no—Mr. Weir: It is unmanly.—Mr. Hall: How do they do in Runcorn.—Mr. Taylor said he was under the impression that a quantity of soil was placed over the coffin, but he was not sure whether the grave was filled up. They had a wooden erection to place over the grave.—Mr.. Aaron said at the cemetery the grave was left open until the next pauper arrived. There was some soil placed over the coffin.—Mr. Weir : If it is done at Runcorn it is a great shame.—A member said it was earning 6s. 2d. easily.—The master (Mr. Cunnah) said every decency was displayed at the House.—The Clerk said he would make inquiries into the subject.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. •

Nominations for Guardians of the Poor for the Runcorn Union do not close until this afternoon Probably Runcorn is the only township where the ratepayers will indulge in the luxury of a contested election, and it is to the public interest that a con- test should take place in these local affairs. It may be taken for granted that the retiring guardians will be nominated, viz., Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. S. Taylor, H. J. Grice, W. Fisher, and P. Speakman, C.C. The last-named gentleman is away on a tour in the Holy Land, and will not return for some weeks, but he is a gentleman whose qualifications for public work are so well known that his absence will not militate against his return. The other gen- tlemen are also well-known and appreciated. . . .

A new element will be introducea into the contest in the shape of a teetotal candidate. The temper- ance party have selected Mr. Thomas Lea to enter ° on their behalf, and there will be an opportunity of gauging the -power of this section of the com- munity. Mr. D. H. Jones, who was last year only defeated by the narrowest of majorities, and un- der circumstances which caused some commotion ot the time, will again appeal tp the ratepayers for their support, and it is also said that Mr. R. Able will offer his services as a guardian of the poor. Altogether there is a prospect of a very lively and interesting election. Widnes is one step nearer the realisation of its ambition. A Local Government Board Commis- sioner, on Wednesday, held an inquiry at the Town Ilan into the application of the Local Board for the charter of incorporation, and Mr. Allen and his assistants had prepared a mass of information necessary for so important an occasion. They were conveyed to the Commissioner through Mr. Squarry, and showed that unpicturesque and smelling as the town might be, it contained a large industrial popu- lation, which through its representatives had acquired a rich and extensive property calculated to add to the comfort and well being of the whole of the 'inhabitants of the town. The town is yearly increasing in importance and material prosperity, and although the Commissioner did not make a definite pronouncement, there were indications showing that the charter asked for would be ' obtained from the Privy Council, who, it was stated would attach no weight to the opposition of the Railway Companies. There can be little doubt that by next November 9th the chemical metropolis will ; contain the dignitaries, Mayor, Aldermen, and Cc.un- cillors.

As the representatives of the Railway Companies feared, there is no doubt that one of the first acts of the Council will be to add to the Town Hall to the present public offices. The Local Board have in their possession the plans of a palatial building, the Central Authority, have sanctioned the borrowing of the requisite money, and no ratepayer will deny that the town is in want of such a building. In fact it is both necessary and desirable.

Yet another fatal accident has occurred on the Runcorn Section of the Ship Canal; and the list is truly becoming an appalling one. The work which is being carried on at Runcorn at thepresent time is of a most important and of a most dangerous character, and yet there is no hospital nearer than Latchford on the one hand and llesmere Port on the other. The man who was injured on Tuesday last, was immediately placed on a loco and conveyed to Latchford, along a railway which is not noted for its smooth running, and probably had he not been unconscious he would have suffered greatly from the jolting he would receive. At any rate, he died a few hours after his admission to the Hospital. Surely,considering the extent and importance of the Runcorn Section and the very large number of men now employed there in dangerous occupations, a hospital ought to be erected where sufferers can receive immediate and efficient attendance. _

- A correspondent last week drew attention to the need of Sunday. trains at Runcorn, and I should like to emphasise his request that, the Commis- sioners will make another effort to obtaia some concession in this respect from the company. tis a lasting shame and a disgrace that any person who may wish to visit friends or relations, on, per- haps, the only day that is free, or who is suddenly called away on some matter of urgent necessity, should be put to the inconvenience of traversing the Bridge,to Widnes railway stations. Besides, why should the Sabbatarian crotchets of a few persons close to the entire population of the town, an easy means of access to the glorious country scenery in the neighbourhood,where one could look up through nature to nature's God, instead of being compelled to remain in a place where the unpicturesque effects of man's defiling hand can be seen in all directions? Lord Halbridge, the present chairman of the Com- pany, is a man of broad principles and sympathies, i and if the matter is represented to him n a clear and impartial manner, he will give effect to the reasonable wishes of the inhabitants.

Local footbaTl-eniiii-Sii-;ts- have been sent into paroxysms of delight this week through the selec- tion of H. Hughes and W. Faulkner tcb play for England against Lancashire next month. The honour in each case is well deserved.

THE AXE-WOUNDING CASE At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, Wm. Henry Sheldon was again brought up on remand charged with assaulting Thomas Rathbone, on the head with an axe, on the 2nd inst.—The Deputy Magistrates' Clerk said the prosecutor was still unable to leave the Infirmary, and applied for a further remand on he same bail as be- fore. The prisoner was remanded accordingly. ON ENCLOSED PREMISES FOR UNLAWFUL PURPOSES. At the Borough Police Court, on Thursday. morning, John Collins, was charged with being found on enclosed premises, 146, Manchester-road, at a quarter to one o'clock that morning, for an unlawful purpose. A con- stable deposed to finding the prisoner in the back yard of a private house at the address mentioned, with a knife and a trowel in his possession, and in company with another man. The back door was open, though it had been locked. Witness arrested the prisoner, but the other man got away. Collins was committed to prison for a month. A DRUNKEN RUFFIAN ASSAULTS A SALVATIONIST. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, John Carney, a labourer, of St. Helens, was charged with being drunk in Hill-st., on Saturday night, also with assaulting Christopher Wilson on the same occasion.—P.C. 8 gave evidence in support of the charges. He said the prose- cutor was walking with the Salvation Army, when the prisoner deliberately drew back, and struck him a violent blow in the face. Witness said he would not allow him to do that, when he threatened to give the prosecutor "some more," and also to assault witness. Thereupon he took him into custody, and he was very rough on the way to the station, kicking witness and dragging him down.—The prosecutor corroborated as to the assault on him, and said he asked the prisoner what he did it for, and he replied "Nothing." Witness said "Won't you apologise ?" and the prisoner answered "No."—The prisoner, who said he belonged to St. Helens, and had come to see the football match, pleaded guilty, and he was sent for a month's hard labour. A BcanntraN YOUTH. At the Borough Police Court, en Wednesday morning, before Mr. J. Fairclough, Joseph Bayne, a lad, said to be 16 years of age, but who, as Mr. Fairclough remarked, did not look more than 14, was charged with being found sleeping on the premises of the White Cross Wire Works Company, early that morning. Police-Sergeant Row- botham said he found the prisoner sleeping in the ash-hole behind the furnace. He told him his mother was dead, and that his father was in prison, but that he had a brother living at 17, Aikin-st.—The prisoner's brother's wife appeared, and said the lad had a good home with them to remain at if he liked, and they had treated him kindly, but he would not stop there. Her husband would not have him back, as they could do nothing with him. The night foreman at the works said the boy could have work there, but he had tried him several times, and he would not stick to it. On the foreman promising that he would do what hecould for the lad, and his sister-in- law that his brother wont(' take him back, the Bench dismissed the case. STREET SAVAGERV.—ASSAULTING A WIFE. At the Warrington Bormigh Police Court, on Monday, John Duain, was charged with assaulting his wife Catherine, in Orford-St., on Saturday night. P.C.'s Corbett and Amson proved the case. The prisoner's wife was running throughthe street with her hair down, flying from her husband, who was chasing her and threatening her life. She appealed to P.C. Corbett to , protect her, and the prisoner having rushed at her and I struck her a most violent blow in the chest, knocking her against the wall, was rushing at her again, when the constable to protect her knocked him down. The woman had now gone out of the way somewhere, as she was afraid of him, he being so cruel to her. The prisoner, a powerful-looking man, said he had not been knocked down, but fell down, that the constable could not have given him a cut he had on his head. P.C. Corbett said that was caused by his coming against the pavement. Alderman Harrison said P.C. Corbett was to be compli- mented on the courageous manner in which he took the woman's part by knocking the prisoner down. There was no doubt that he would have murdered her but for this.—The prisoner was sent to gaol for two months' hard labour.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—The following persons were dealt with for being drunk and disorderly :—Maggie Dooley, in Mersey-at., on Saturday night, fined ss. and costs.—Patrick Geoghegan, in Bridge-st., on Sunday night, 10s. and costs.—Martin Cohen was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Sunday night, in Pinner's Brow, in which street he lodged, also with threatening the life of his landlady, Annie White, and fined 20s. and costs.—Thomas Glavin, drunk and disorderly in Bank-st., on the 14th inst., was fined 10s. and costs.—Jane Hennessy, in Buttermarket-st., on the 16th, and 17th inst., 2s. 6d. and costs in each case.—James Jackson, hod carrier, from Manchester, in Winwick-st., on Satur- day night, ss. and costs.—Robert Fogg and John Fleming, in Lime-st., on Saturday night, 2s. 6d. each. RUGBY. ST. HELENS RECREATION V. IV ARRINGTON.—(THIRD TEAMS.)—In this match, played at Warringtan on Satur- day, simultaneously with the first team match, the home- sters had it all their own way. Alkett got two tries, Hansom and Russell one each, while William Warburton kicked three goals. Final result—Warrington, 3 goals, 1 try, 5 minors; St. Helens Recreation, 1 minor. WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND V. WIDNES OLD BOYS.—The return fixture between these teams took place on the ground of the former on Saturday, the home team beitig poorly represented. The visitors kicked off, and at once took play to the home lines' where the game raged for some time, but by combined play the Rangers cleared to neutral ground. The Old Boys, however, were not to be denied, for after some loose play the ball was kicked over the line, and Lavin rushing up secured a try for the visitors. Half time being called, the score read—Old Boys 1 try, Rangers, 2 minors. Upon the restart the homesters played' up strongly, but by nice passing the visitors cleared, and White ran in a good try, the kick at goal again failing. From the drop out the home team got well into their opponents' quarters. Appleton from a scrimmage broke away and scored a clever try in a • good position. Cook, however, made a poor attempt at goal. The Rangers were now having the best of it, Hamer from a free kick, far out, making a splendid bid for goal, the ball striking the bar, and rebounding into play. The game continued to be very exciting, but the Old Boys eventually retired victors by 2 tries, 2 minors to the Rangers 1 try, 4 minors. RUNCORN V. LIVERPOOL OLD Boys—The return match between these teams on Saturday at Liverpool drew together a large body of spectators. Representing the Runcorn team were—S. Houghton, back ;T. H. Davies, H. May, and G. Pendlebury, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes and S. Abrams,half backs ; W.Hughes,G.Webbe, H. Williams,?. Riley, A. Hampson, J. Davies. J. Gayter, W. Broady, and C. Hughes, forwards. The Old Boys' team was composed of—W. Hilton; back; W. H. Male, H. D. Wood, and W. Legge, three-quarter backs ; J. B. O'Dwyer and A. R. Harrison, half backs; R. P. Wilson, 11. C. Wood, E. W. Bullen,R. L. Armour, J. J. S. Rowe, H. R. Townsend, W. Smellie, R. M`Turk, and L. Cham- bers, forwards. On behalf of the home team O'Dwyer put the ball into motion, and the play for a short time was somewhat uninteresting, until Runcorn broke away and Davies gave signs of causing the Old Boys some trouble. The saving clause was only just put in at the right moment ; but the Runconians still pressed their opponents to the line. From a scrimmage May obtained possession from Abrams,and dropped a magnificent goal. Some spirited play followed, the passing of the home team being grand ; but the defensive tactics were too much for the "Boys," and no advantage was secured. Abrams and Pendlebury then showed good form, and W. Hughes took a free kick at centre, which fell some- what short. Pressure was brought to bear ; and Davies scored a try, which was converted into a fine goal from near to touch. Even play succeeded this, and, owing to Davies being disabled,play was stopped for some inimites, Davies having retired from the game, Gayter took the three-quarter position. The visitors, although a man short, forced the play, and a free kick was conceded, the cliim being made owing to the ball being picked out of the scrimmage. At half-time the score stood—Run- corn, 2 goals; Old Boys, nil. On the resumption of play Harrison was collared before he could return. After scrimmaging, Herbert Wood broke away; but Legge failed to receive a pass, and the visitors resumed the attack, H. Hughes p.nd May being the most prominent. Abrams and Houghton played also with much dash, and after some fine play and brilliant passing, Chambers obtained a try behind the posts. Wood, however, failed to convert, the ball rebounding from the post. The Old Boys were somewhat spurred on by this piece of play, and Male and Harrison essayed drops at goal, but signally failed. Wood almost got over ' • but Houghton who was on the alert, brought him up. A rush by Run- corn followed, and Gayter obtained a chance but was prevented from doing any further mischief. day crossed the line; but Houghton failed to score. A minor was forced by Runcorn just before time was called, and the score stood at the finish—Runcorn, 2 goals, 1 try, 2 minors ; Old Boys, 1 try. WARRINGTON A v. ST. HELENS RECREATION A.—This encounter was contested on the Saints' ground on Satur- day, the ground being in first class condition and all in favour of an open game. Grainger on behalf of the Recreation opened the combat. Thornley charging the kick, play was quickly fluttering on the home lines,until ' Gerrard cameaway to the quarter flag. A struggle here ended in 'I hornley getting away and passing to Knowles, but some time elapsed before either side could gain any advantage, although Mather, intercepting a pass, raced away to the quarter flag. A couple of grand pieces of work by Jolley completely nullified all the efforts on the part of the homesters,and a fine cross dribble by Lawless and Knbwles ended in a minor, another quickly follow- ing. Directly after this the home team raced away to the visitors' 25, where Lally put in a brilliant run, only to see the advantage neutralized by strong forward play. A brief attack by Davies, Craghan, Lloyd, and Povey was spoiled by Mees, and after Sampson had cleared his lines, the home team were penalized for off-side. Some vigorous kicking between the backs was succeeded by another fine run by Lally, and a capital bit of pas- sing between Lawless, Lally, and Potts ended in the latter running over. At last, the Warrington forwards, who were now playing splendidly together, worked the leather to midfield, where, after some sharp passing, the ball fell into the willing hands of Lally, who effected another brilliant run, the outcome being that Jolley threw wide to Daniels, who romped over. The drop-out was of no avail, for a powerful burst, headed by Teare, Barnes, Buckley and Davies, forced the sphere to the line, and after a determined attack, Lawless threw out to Jolley, who rushed over under the posts, Davies con- verting' and Warrington crossed over with 1-2-2 to the good. Jolley for the visitors restarted, and the ball had not long been in motion when this player effected a magnificent run, and threw to Buckley, who was how- ever, bowled over before he could cross, Briers relieving the danger by a capital dribble. Then the Warrington forwards combining beautifully worked the leather to the Rees' 25,!and from a fair catch Sampson made a very fine bid for goal. The drop out found play hovering about mid-fieN, the advantage being further enhanced by Mather's run and kick, and the visitors were pressed. A kick being charged, Lloyd, Cragan, Barnes and Teare dribbled away, and a series of tremendoug punts by Jolley followed. Some rough and tumble tussels were hereabouts fought,and after a very smart bit by Daniels, a magnificent rush by the whole of the Warrington for- wards ended in Lawless 'scoring. The next item was a run by Lally, who passed to Lawless, and being supple- mented by a rush from Povey, the home lines were again in danger. Mees proved the saviour of his side, but his efforts were nullified by Sampson, and in close follow- ing to a dribble,by Thornley,Povey, Davies and Knowles, Lawless ran in a good try and Sampson kicked a goal. A smart bit of play by Potts on restarting was succeeded by Daniels dodging his opponents splendidly, and an- other powerful rush by the Warringtonians saw Davies getting possession, and after a most determined rush get a try, which Sampson improved. Shortly afterwards Lally wound up the scoring by running over at the corn- er flag, and Warrington a:venging their only defeat re- tired winners by 3 goals 4 tries 5 minors to nil. WIDNES v. ASPULL.

Widnes journeyed to Aspull on Saturday, to play off the return fixture with the club of that name, and suc- ceeded in recording another victory, which they fully deserved. After some pressure by the home team, Hartles, who was in excellent form, relieved, and the home back failing to return, play settled in the centre of the field. The ball was gradually worked into the Wid- nes quarter, yvhere for obstruction by one of the visitors Aspull was given a penalty kick in an easy position for goal. Pilkington took the place kick, and the ball was sent flying between the uprights, the point being re- ceived with enthusiastic cheers. Widnes kept Aspull on the defensive for some few minutes, wlien two beautiful passes between Evans and Barber resulted in Drummond dropping a splendid goal. Roberts relieved with a short run, but Brennan and Peters opposed his progress. Anderton now attempted to drop at goal, but only a minor resulted. From the drop out Widnes attacked, but half time arrived with the scere Widnes one goal, to
