Aspull one goal and two minors. On changing ends the game was most uninteresting. Widnes had slightly the advantage, and for a full quarter of an hour pinned the home team ons,&heir own lines, but only three minors were placed to the credit of the Widnes score. The game ended in a victory for Widnes, the score being Widnes one goal (dropped) and three minors, to Aspull one goal _ _

(petialty)' and ihree minors. WARRINGTON v. LANCASTER. With the view of giving the Lancaster club a helping hand owing to the losses they have sustained during the recent severe frost, the Warringtonians journeyed to Lancaster on Monday afternoon. The Warrington team differed in three instances from that which so gallantly lowered the St. Helens Recreation colours, Daniels taking
the place of Webster at three-quarters, whilst Davies and Thorniley officiated in place of Jolley and Holmes. The first match this season resulted in a heavy score being

piled on against the Northerners, and although they did I not expect to gain the verdict on the present occasion, I they were fully confident of reducing tl.e original large I score put on against them. An average" gate" was recorded, and at 5.50 Mcßoberts started, Boscow directing the reply to the half-way flag. The leather was worked to the Warrington end, and a succession of scrimmages ultimately resulted in favour of the homes- ters. The bold front presented by the Lancaster men astonished the rather too sanguine Warringtonians, and a rush, headed by Ashton and Thorniley, was further aided by Evans making his mark, a tremendous kick sending the oval to near the home line. Cowell got the oval away smartly, and then Fair Turner, with a strong rush down the open, found Beasdale saving in plucky, fashion. The Lancaster forwards asserted their super- iority in a marked manner, and Winn and Garth, with an extra effort, once more pressed the Warrington team back. Desultory play followed, until Boscow raised a cheer with a clever kick. Not to be denied,the homesters returned to the attack, and Winder looked a certain scorer before James Bate appeared on the scene, and pulledhim up Thorniley and J. T. Bate were especially prominent in a relief, and following this came an excellent run by James Bate, who dodged in grand style, but he held the oval just a trifle too long, and the Lancaster goal escaped disaster. A penalty kick to each side ruled play at neutral ground, and although James Bate again shone with a dribble, he received but poor assistance, and a chance was thrown away. So far, the Warringtonians had shown nothing like a glimpse of their proper form, and the forwards being a trifle disorganised, Carter headed a rush of the home team, and Parkinsod dropped

at goal, which found Boscow saving. A grand run-by Barnes, immediately after the drop-out, was duly ap- plauded, but the first twenty minutes ended with the score as a minor to nil in favour of Lancaster. For the first quarter of an hour in the second half the play was of the tamest description. Although play was generally confined to the Lancaster quarters, there was a laxity of that dash which has been recently such a prominent fea- ture. of the Warringtonians' play, and there did seem a .probability of the match terminating in a draw. But the visitors had evidently the measure of their opponents, and near the call of time, a grand display by the Bates and Evans resulted in the latter punting high to Lam- bert. The latter, in his anxiety to clear, was at fault, and from a scrimmage on the line, J. T. Bate secured and darted over. Evans was entrusted with the place, and landed a goal. The remaining /items were of a give-and- take nature, and the final score read as—Warrington, 1.0-1; Lancaster, 0-0-1. Lancaster team :—II. Lambert, back; Cowell, Hartley, and Bleasdale, three-quarters ; Lambert, Parkinson, and Garth, half backs; Gilson, Winder, Kitchen, Winn Herbert, Crook, Pinch, and Mcßoberts, forwards. Referee, Mr. Pollitt, Swinton. WARRINGTON V. ST. HELENS RECREATION. Ever since October 25th last, when the Warringtonians received such a castigation at the hands of the St. Helens Recreation, the return match has been awaited with in- terest, and there was no wonder at the tremendous gate which assembled at Wilderspool on Saturday. Before the last-named day, Warrington had never been able to lower the Saints' colours, and of the four matches played the Recreation had Won two, whilst the remainder had been left undecided. It was only to be expected that our local team would make a bold effort, and how they gallantly achieved their object on Saturday was ,indeed something remarkable. Their efforts had been reserved for one great essay in the last stage of the game, and fertune shiniag on them for once in a way, the match was pulled out of the fire in the last three minutes, and Warrington hailed victors. It was estimated that 7,000 lined the arena, and of this number 1,500 journeyed from St: Helens. Both sides played as originally selected, and a round of applause welcomed each team as they made their ap- pearance some twenty minutes late. The stiffish breeze caused the game to be divided into four quarters, and Parr winning the choice of ends took advantage of the elements. The opening exchanges took place between Elligon and Barnes, and although half way was the scene of operations, a couple of fine kicks by nodgson and Seddon gave the Saints a decided advantage. However, the Warrington defence stood the test well, and Barnes, aided by his experience, relieved with capital judgment. and this effort being augmented by a rush, in which Berry, Jolley. and Donohue were prominent, the centre flag was reached. Not to be denied, the visitors once more got possession,a,nd Pyke was alnaost in from a rush, Boscow pulling him up near the line. The oval was speedily passed to Seddon, but Barnes was,on him like a dart, and Donohue and the two Bates dribbling well, Webster and Evans each kicked finaly, and for the first time the Recs.' quarter flag was reached. A passing bout by the home half backs was frustrated, and from some fluctuating play the tall kicking of the visiting backs proved of immense value, and Seddon and Ellison by this means transferred the game to the home end. Barnes, Evans, and the Bates defended admirably, and, although Jolley and Fair. Turner, by smart following up averted disaster for the, time being, Ellison did some tricky work on the popular side, and from smart play Turton passed to Pilkington,who baffled thehome backs, and scored under the posts. Seddon made a sorry exhi- bition with the place. Warrington played up pluckily on the restart, and Barnes came in for a round of ap- plause for his exact tackling of Seddon. Ashton led his men in fine style in a rush to the Saints' 25, and Holmes and Dillon were very prominent with useful work. A couple of fair were, sufficed to change the venue, and J. T. Bate saved in daring style on one occa- sion when disaster seemed probable. However, the first quarter was ended, and Warrington had now the advantage of the wind, which had slightly subsided. The play opened in the home quarters, but Barnes and Evans soon had the oval out of danger, and some fine passing took the oval beyond half way. Fair Turner struggled from a line out and partially got free, but the two Bates and Jolley dribbling effectively, the Recs.' goal was in jeopardy. Jackson put in a poor response. and another sequence ef passes between Fair Turner, J. T. Bate, James Bate, and Webster saw Jackson being tackled under the posts. Frank Turner was foremost in the rush over the line, but the kick was a trifle too hard, and only a minor was recorded. Sharp passing by the home half-backs again puzzled the visitors, but Seddon luckily got in his kick, and although Webster failed at the first attempt to reply, he recovered himself finely and got his kick in under difficulties. A fine display of pas- sing by the home backs was foiled by Ellison, who took the game too near the Warrington2s, but the attack was only momentary, for Dillon, Randles, and Fair Turner rushed the oval back. Another display by the Bates, Barnes, and Evans saw the latter dropping at goal and registering the second minor. Exchanges between Bos- cow, James Bate, Webster' Seddon, and Jackson ended with a distinct advantage to the homesters, and from some loose play Berry got in, but the try was,disallowed. A long kick by Boscow saw Jackson scoring for the third time, and half time was then called, with the score—Re- creation, 0-1.0; Warrington, 0-0-3. The last stages of the game were confined to fifteen minutes each, and the homesters, having this fact in view, made the pace a cracker right from the kick off. Defensive tactics were early adopted by the visitors, and although the oval was got away to Boscow, the home custodian was brilliant in his kicking. James Bate got smartly away from a pack, and Barnes passed a little too high for Evans, or a certain score would have resulted. An excursion was paid to the home quarters, by the aid of Hodgson and Pyke, and the former nearly scored from a running pas- sing movement, Holmes saving a certain try. The attack was but brief, and fine play by Webster, J. T. Bate, Frank Turner, and Bandies soon had the oval on the Saints' lines. Jolley was especially prominent on the popular side, and J. T. Bate raised a hope when he got clear, but failed to hold the oval. Not a point was scored during this quarter, and ends were changed and War- rington were in a minority. The Saints now appeared to show a laxity in their work, the fast nature at which the contest had been waged undoubtedly told on them, for on the restart a determined onslaught was made on the visitors' goal. Jackson early conceded a minor, and Jolley and Donohue were to the fore with beautiful work. Six minutes to play and Warrington on the losing side, and then a bold effort was made. The homesters had evidently recovered their energies, for a final effort saw Jolley making headway, and then from a combined rush the oval was worked over and Ashton made the scores equal. Turner failed at the difficult place. It was not too late yet for Warrington to win the match, and the Recs. playing like a beaten team, the homesters again pressed, and in the next minute J. T. Bate was single-handed in a dribbling movement, and a loud cheer announced a try, Evans kicking a grand goal from a difficult angle. Evans made a bold bid a moment later, and Frank Turner almost landed a goal from a fair catch by Boscow. This was the last point of the match and the game terminated—Warrington, 1-1.6; St. Helens Recreation, 0-1-0. Teams :—Warrington: Boscow, back ; Webster, Evans, and Barnes, three-quarter backs; James Bate, and J. T. Bate, half backs; Ashton, Fair Turner. Frank Turner, Jolley, Berry, Holmes, E. Dillon, Bandies and Donohue, forwards. St. Helens Recreation: T. R. Jackson, back: J. Ellison' J. Seddon, and T. Hodgson, three-quarter backs; J.Turton, and J. Pilkington, half backs ; W. Parr, J. Pyke, J. Dolan, J. Mousdale, J. Hankinson, E. Fildes, W. Dean, T: Reynolds, T. Winstanley, and R. Fildes, forwards. Referee, Mr. Bleackley, Manchester.
ASSOCIATION.

WAURINGTON ASSOCIATION V. GA.RSTON L. AND N.- W. R. —These teams met at Arpley, in grand weather, on Saturday. The visitors kicked off against the wind, but the home team getting possession soon made tracks for the Garston end, a free kick being awarded close in goal from which J. Mather notched the first point, five minutes from the start. After this play was more evenly ' contested, each end being visited in turn. Clayton and Ball showed up well with some fine runs on the right Wing, as also did Smith in goal. Close on half time,the visitors getting close in, they secured their only goal from a mistake by the home backs, thus bringing half time with one goal each. After the re-start give-and-take ensued, until a shot from Ball enabled Powell to score another goal for the Warringtonians. This roused the home team to renewed vigour, and they severely taxed the railway men's defence, their backs and goalkeeper playing a splendid game. The home team tried hard to score, and were at last rewarded with another goal from the foot of Powell, thus winning a fast and exciting; game for Warrington by 3 goals te Garston 1. War- rington team :—Goal, Smith; full backs, Phillips and Davies ; half backs, Ayling, J. Mather, and Parry (cap.); forwards, Ball, Clayton, Cornforth, Powell, and T. Mat- her. Referee, Mr. T. Jones.

FOOTBALL.-RUGBY.

Something like -,--stirprise was provided by the third round for the Yorkshire Cup. This was nothing less than the downfall of Bradford at Park Avenue. After their splendid performances this season it is safe to assume that such a contingency was never contemplated by Bradford. To be knocked out by Halifax was quite unexpected, and it affords one more proof of the uncer- tainty of cup ties. The victory was largely due to the wonderful place-kicking of Barnes, who converted a couple of tries into goal from the touch line. The home team could not score at all until the last ten minutes, when Jenkinson ran in and Doyle landed a goal. The news of the turn-up created a sensation in the evening. Huddersfield had a hard task with Dewsbury, only beat- ing them by a single try.
The competition for the South-east Lancashire Cup has reached the semi-finalltage,and the trophy seems to once more lie at the mercyla Ratcliffe.

Several matters of importance were dealt with by the Rugby Union at its meetina in London, on Tuesday. Motions were on the agenda from Yorkshire, Lancashire, and Devonshire to alter the present method of scoring, but before they were brought forward the Chairman suggested that it was a matter for the International Board, and the gentlemen whose names were down for the motions withdrew them, the Chairman proposing, and Mr. G. Rowland Hill seconding, the following re- solution :—" That the International Board be asked to consider the question of scoring during the stimmer, and to issue a report on the subject previous to the month of September.' The Rev. F. Marshall explained that the opinion of the Yorkshire Committee was that a try should count one, a goal however obtained, except for a penalty kick, two points, to be added to the try, and a goal from a penalty kick should count one point. Mr. Marshall thought a dropped goal by no means so meri- torious as a goal got by a try. Mr. Arthur Budd con- sidered a dropped goal one of the best and prettiest points in the game. In the end the Chairman's resolu- tion was agreed to without a division. Mr. W. Cail pro- posed, and Mr. H. Vassall seconded, a resolution striking out rules 8 and 13, and altering 12 to read "A player when on-side may take up the ball any time except, in a scrimmage." This motion, which abotishes the dead ball, was carried.

'The Rev. F. Marshall proposed, and Mr. J. H. Payne seconded "That the Union Committee be requested to make such alterations and additions to the regulations relating to professionalism as shall prevent the illegal importation of players." The proposer could not conceal from himself that veiled professionalism very largely existed in Yorkshire, and sooner or later would have to be dealt with. Another question of importance was that of payment for loss of time, Which was being earnestly discussed in the north of England. He only mentioned these matters in connection with this resolution, be- cause he wanted the Union to be ahead of professionals instead of letting the question get in front of them as did their brethren of the Association code. The resolution was carried.

Mr. G. Rowland Hill ,announce that the Committee had been in communication with the hon. secretary of the Western Province (Rugby Union), South Africa, and said that if a team could be raised it would go out there for a fifty days' tour in June next. It was also announced that the match of the Champion County (Lancashire) v. Rest of England would take place at Manchester on April 18.

That they are pretty keen on football in South Africa is shown by the communication which has been received by Mr. Rowland Hill. The Western Province Rugby Football Union are prepared to guarantee £2,000 at once, leaving £l,lOO to be paid by the Transvaal and Natal districts as actual expenses. It is expected by the Colonists that a first-class team will be sent out, that the tour will extend over seventy days, and that it will take place during the months of July and August.

div.p: ASSOCIATION.

There was the usual crowd at the Oval on Saturday, to see the final tie for the English Association Cup between Blackburn Rovers and Notts, a vast number of excur- sionists journeying up to London from the Midlands, whilst several hundreds took advantage of the trips from Lancashire. They were rewarded by seeing one of the finest contests in the history of the competition. There was more than the customary mystery surrounding the probable result. Notts had plaxed in such gallant style against Sunderland in the semi-final,and had a few days before scored such a sensational victory over the Rovers at Blackburn, that they were established the favourites. The Rovers had been going to pieces recently, and there were doubts-about Southworth being in the team, owing to a strained leg. All the circumstances combined to make the issue very uncertain. The Blackburn section ef the crowd were especially anxious until the players had fallen to work, but their minds were soon set at ease. The Rovers looked like winning almest right off, and they wound up triumphant for the fifth time in their career.

The benefit of experience was plainly manifest. The Rovers played just as well as if they had been at home among their own supporters, but it cannot be said that Notts were seen at their best until well on in the second half,when their chance was practically hopeless. Thraves was not so smart or steady in goal as he had been in the preceding rounds, and the defence was less sound. Nor did the forwards get along in that dashing fashion which won the day at Sheffield. On the other hand,the Rovers' front rank made many telling runs,and shot at goal with much more effect. Whilst Southworth was not up to his best, the wings acquitted themselves with credit,Townley quite taking the fancy of the spectators. Brandon and Forbes were a long :ivay safer than Hendry and Ferguson, the magnificent way in which they cleared the goal being often cheered. Pennington, who was substituted for "Gow, did fairly well in goal, but he has as yet ago od deal to learn. The Rovers have now equalled the per- formance of the London Wanderers in winning the cup five times.

shall be glad if you will kindly allow me, in gottrnext issue, to correct an error. Oil Saturday last in your report of my remarks at the lecture on " Mendelssohn " by Mr. Crossley, you reported ine:to have said that "Mr. L. W. Reynolds paid the deficiencies of the Musical Society out of his own pocket," or to this effect. I must have said so, for two different reporters could not have made the same mistake. What Wa-s in my mind, and what I intended to say, was that "Mr. Reynolds' advanced the deficiencies out of his own , pocket," which is a very different thing; because all . such deficiencies were ultimately discharged by the few staunch supporters of the Society. I regret that I (un- wittingly) stated what, I knew, was not in accordance with the fact.—Yours truly, Lower Walton, 21,3, 1891.
GEORGE WOODS.

div.head: SUNDAY TRAINS FOR RUNCORN.
div.p: SUNDAY TRAINS FOR RUNCORN.

Sir,--Public attention is once more drawn to this -matter. lam sure lam only one of a large number of townspeople who sincerely hope, with "Pro Bono Pub- lico," that our Commissioners will again take this ques- tion in hand. Surely this town has been long enough debarred the privilege enjoyed by other towns of having Sunday trains. Why should the Runcorn pecple who want to take train be compelled to walk to Widnes every Sunday, and vice versa, as they now are'? It is well known that it is no joke to walk over the bridge in inclement weather, to 'say nothing of the disagreeable and tiresome walk through Widnes,but it has to be done every Sunday throughout the year, foul or fair, by those who travel by rail. Is it fair to Runcorn ?—Yours Sze., 'vox. Runcorn. March 25th, 1891.

div.head: HINT FOR BOYS-AND MEN, TOO.
div.p: A HINT FOR BOYS-AND MEN, TOO.

Sir,—ln looking over a contemporary of yours the other day, I came across the following 'letter, which I thought you might be inclined to reprint for the benefit of the rising generation. The letter deals with e. subject that is forcing itself to the front, and Will presently have to be dealt with by Parliament, The habit of smoking has become so very prevalent that it is well at times to listen to observant individuals such as-" Prognosticator ;" and thoughtful youths may study his remarks with advantage. Yours, Sze.,
ANTI-TOI3'ACCONIST,

E.E.xtracti]. After watching and studying tobacco smoking for nearly sevente/ years the following has beentthe result I find produced :—First. It carries boys out of.their natural sphere, and creates in them an artificial thirst (it has this effect both upon men and boys), that generally leads to drinking. Second. It has a decided tendency to make People lazy. Third. It interferes with nature in married life. Fourth. Its action upon the system, though often- times very slow,is always sure; at other times it-is much quicker, and many minds and intellects are imbeciled much earlier in life than in others. Fifth. It affects the eyesight very much. In some cases people have become blind, others have weak eyes, and are obliged to wear glasses, particularly the rising generation,and they don't know the cause. Sixth. It very often produces cancer in the throat and mouth, and many cases 'have proved fatal. Seventh. It is a useless, expensive habit, and no. good can arise from it
PROGNOSTICATOR.

div.head: "GOING THE WHOLE HOG."
div.p: "GOING THE WHOLE HOG."

Sir,—l was glad to see Anti-i'ish's 'letter. "I like it. and would point out two other kinds .of Objectionable' food. Firstly, vegetables.—All the vegetables we eat are, so to speak, scavengers of the soil. Is not their ,principal, form of nourishment the excrement collected from dwell- ing-houses, stables, cow-houses, pig-styes &c. and some- times even rotten fish from overstocked markets? Let anyone ask a rhubarb grower with what he manures his rhubarb—perhaps he would tell-: let him • ascertain what potatoes are chiefly grown with: let him go to some sewage farm and see the cabbages, turnips,' &c., flourish- ing there; and then let him reflect what he is in reality masticating when in the act of eating such things. Depend upon it no vegetables are fit for human consump- tion; therefore they should be excluded from our dietary. Secondly, with regard to fleShmeat.—Birds and beasts are either scavengers directly, for instance, duCks, geese, "popular" pigs, &c. or—which amounts to the same thing—subsist on scavengers, i.e. vegetation. Flesh, then, cannot be fit forbuman food, and should be rigor- ously avoided. People cannot be too careful what they eat, and I feel sure that if everybody would discard these two classes of food, together with that mentioned by Anti-fish, they would be far different people to what they are. Perhaps someone will kindly explain what -we ought not to drink eating is my strong point.—Yours &C., SQUBABIISH.

div.head: INE-FISII-lENCT OF ." ANTI-FISH."
div.p: THE INE-FISII-lENCT OF ." ANTI-FISH."

Sir,—The ill-considered rhodomontade of your corres- pondent," Anti-fish," must surely be the reflection of a nightmare, the creation of a too heavy anti-fish supper. This letter illustrates the maxim that ignorance is al- ways fearful of shadows. A little knowledge is said to be a dangerous thing; it certinly is disquieting in the case of "Anti-fish." Had he carried his morbid investi- gations sufficiently far he might have found relief from his ichthynpbobi ain the fact that all that he eats is the product of dead organisms. The poor man is not suffi- ciently far-seeing for his own comfort. Does he take refuge in vegetables? Potatoes and cabbage are essen- tially gross feeders, they delight in alimentary abomina- tions. Had " Anti-fish " but the wisdom and the kneew- ledge required to trace the materials of his own y resent body back to their sources, he might then see reasons for the acceptance of the inevitable, and so cease to nastily° .his diseased imagination upon such ghastly details. In him the most patent facts are hidden by a distorted pre- judice. He dislikes fish ; hence it is tastele.vs and innutri- tious ! The almost exclusively fish4ed poptilation our ••c9oasts can not be evidenced in support of this th‘ory ! A fish diet is said to be productive of brisinen In your correspondent's abstention may we not trace a•cause and an effect, in the deduction of silly conclusions from un- sound premises ?--.1 am, &c., March 21, 189 L
JOHN PEERS.
"GAS" V. COMMON SENSE.

Sir,—There is no pleasing those canting teetotal professors. I penned my last letter. as I thought., up to the full level of their understanding, and I cannot drag my language lower even to suit them. Therete "four Richmonds in the field" now, .and it is difficult to select the one that contains the most trash. " Veritag" says I must have been highly excited when I penned ms- last letter, but he never more misjudged sven a brewer! "On-looker" has incubated a few lines, which have-taken a fortnight to hatch; and, when hatched, they only go to show that he wants te be con- -sidered a judge of taste, which he certainly is not. ," Master of Ails " poses as a logician, and selects "mid- dens "as the source of his logic! Sir, I feel that he is quite at home there, and as you " cannot touch pitch without being defiled," I let him drop, the more readily that, whatever I wrote, he would garble and twist my meaning, as befcr,te. Poor "Felix," however, deserves a little, more atten- tion. He thinks lam suffering from softening of the brain, principally, lfancy, because I asserted, and now calmly re-assert, that there are brewers who have done more to ameliorate the condition of their fellowmen, yes, with snly the scratch of a pen, than all the Hughes's in existeskce have eves..done, or ever will! It is one thing—and a very cheap one—to get into a pulpit and fulminate against drink for the sake of pleasing such out-and-out fanatics as "Felix ;" but when all is done, , and the man has said his worst, there is not a single sufferer gets a farthing out of him ; but "words, empty words," are the only solace he has for them. Give me man who pats his hand in his pocket, and gives material help to those who need, in preference to the one who has nothing but fine speeches to offer. . _ . .
- -And, acting on the dvice of "Felix," I have seriously pondered the qiptation from John W.egley, and Ifillould

not thank him if I were a Wesleyan for dragging to light such an over-powering proof of the delirium that will affect even the best of us, when bigotry gets the mastery over us. Sir, logic and cant are two useful things in their way ; but they are sadly wanting in value when weighed against good, solid, material gifts and I have only to express my surprise that even my Tour puerile opponents can't see it. They are so deep in theory, that they can't or irox't realize what it is to practise : " So have I seen, tit black and white, &prating thing, a magpie hight, Majestically stalk; A rtately, worth,ess animal. That plies the tongue, and wagt thetail, AU flutter, pride, and talk I" 23,3,1891.

IN DARKEST IGNORANCE, RPM MOSES; INTO THE DAWN WITHOUT HIM. "It thus becOmes a problem for us—Whether we shall accept whet we know is be trite even if that acceptance shoul, in- volve the rejection of what we once imagined to be true, or, on the other hand, shall we give up the hard-earned fruits of modern investigation—the result of rigorously logical in- duction from well ascertained facts, and return to the simple faith of.our forefathers, knowing that this can only be, and bejustified, by a complete recurrence to the state of com- parative ignorance of that age; the faith in fact being only possildEP in conjunction with the want of knowledge."— Sunday School Manual, X.D. 2091. Sir,—ln foregoing letters we have seen it made suffi- ciently 'evident, that, if Moses was inspired, it must have been by some such spirit as that cited in 11. Ch. XVIII., 22. 'But need we thaw upon this suppositiously super- natural source of information? Little need to appeal to inspiration—veracious or other—when we find an almost identical fable current among a people who flourished some 2000 years before the bilyih of Moses The Shumiro- Accadians—the precursors of the Chalchens—have left 'us-some most curious and interesting records of their belief. In the British Museum, the letter impressed clays—in cylinders and tablets—bear undoubted evidence 'of the working of the imagination of some old Accadiaa "Moses, who has thus anticipated his Mosaic plagiarist by over 1000 years. In these records we have a circum stanial account of the Creation—the Temptation and the Fall, with its proper appendages of seductive apples and a whispering serpent, which latter event some Accadian artist in clay has graphically depicted—thus giving "confirmation " stronger " than proof from Holy Writ" of the pre-Mosaic existence of these fables. In fact Moses has been cabbaging " both plot and characters from his earlier brother in the Teligious story-telling line, and unblushingly appropriating to his own use and for his own aggrandisement in the eyes of his simple followers— a pre-existing narrative, equally idle and equally fabu- lous.

What -wonder then that *a -narrative that begins by literary larceny, and an impious and self-invalidated assumption of D ivine direction, should continue in error and blundering mis-statements ? For instance we have metal working and an instructor therein during the life of the first man! Here we have Moses still in the dark or wilfully suppressing the fact that primitive men had .no knowledge of the use ofmetals,but worked flints and other hard stones into tools and weapons. The entire absence of any hint as to -such a period in man's history as that of the stone-age, lasting as it did for very many generations, would of itself be entirely destructive of the idea of the historic accuracy of any author dealing thus with the early history of his race. How much more so, then, one who transcends even this negative evidence by a piece of positive evidence of the entire ab- sence,alike of special knowledge and Divine information, on this subject. But the fact of the great stone-age, though unknown to, or-suppressed by, Moses is inferen- tially attested to by the Bible itself in "the sharp stone" used in circumcision. Here we have evidence that the Jews, as a Conservative people, fond of old customs and observances, had retained the use of a flint tool in their religious rites long after it had lost the fore of impera- tive necessity. In this retention we have a custom left standing like a geologic out-her—the sole memento of some long gone epoch. And yet the divinely inspired Moses makes the first metal worker contemporary with the first man! Here I do not accuse this narrator of plagiarism; this, at least, may be his own. Again, the chronology of Moses is quite Mosaic.. It makes the world 50me,433 years old at the time of the bulrush episode. Archeology and geology alike agree in asserting that a very much longer period must have intervened between the first man and the Pharaahs. By-the-by where is our old friend Biblical chronology now ? We are told there is no such thing now ! But there was once a Biblical chronology Usshered into the world by a biblical midwife hailing from Dublin. But alas! this interesting babe was short lived. It died by exposurp to adverse facts which brought on a severe fit of acute criticism under which it succumbed. After paying a passing tribute of a sigh to the memory of this . child of Mosaic afflatus, we may note that, though the deduction may be dead and buried, the statements from -which it was drawn are still where they were and as valid as ever; a stumbling block to the believer and an evi- dence to the untrammelled thinker of the entire untrust- worthiness of Moses in this and like subjects. And this view of the matter is in no wise invalidated by the supposition that-Moses did not originate these fables and false statements. Whoever it was drew up the Decalogue, adopted these tales and mis-statements ; and /by such adtfption made himself a participant in, and responsible for such errors and falsities. And this re- sponsibility dogs the footsteps of every subsequent adop- ter who also makes claim to supra-human nature. What then are the conclusions we come to by the considera- tion of this and other points noticed? One I think is this —the entire ignorance and untrustworthiness of Moses in matters outside human experience; and hence that he was either deluded himself or was a deluder of others. If I am asked—what then becomes of the Redemption, there having been no Fell? I answer unhesitatingly as it is with the foundation, so it will fare with what is built on it! If Apocalyptic Christianity is built on this founda- tion, it must share the fate of its foundation, and stand or fall therewith. I hereappend a synopsis of the argu- ments used, and invite-your readers to give them the most rigorous examination compatible with logical treat- ment. As an ignoramus in Hebrew, I must assume the general accuracy of the Revised Version, and, as an acceptor of the first canon: of literary criticism, adhere strictly to its text. This being premised I find : L The book opens with an assumption of prehuman , history. involving supernatural knowledge equivalent to dieineinspiration or instruction. IL This claim to divine guidance is quickly invali- dated by Ist, a statement ,which we knowto be unt.rue, as to the time taken up in creation. 2nd, as to the method of that creation which runs quite counter to the logical deductions from well Ascertained facts in natural history. 3rd by the negative and positive evidente of the writer's ignorance of the prevalence of the great stone-age, to the existenceof which the Bible itself bears unconscious testimony. 4th, by the utterly inadequate and scientifically condemned mosaic chronology. 111. Whether these fables and misstatements originated with Moses or were copies, he adopted them, and so in- dorsed and became responsible for what of error they contain. IV. This responsibility applies equally to all subse- quent adopters who claim superhuman nature. V. -If Apocalyptic Christianity is founded on the Fall of Man from a state of primitiveinnocence,it is a delusion foundetton a fable. . Finally, as a conce,ssion to our weaker brethren who , may not be able to see beyond the arguments used, I. .wish to say that in no way or instance can the foregoing be rightly taken as antagonistic to true religion, or to the active existence of that "Power., not ourselves, that makes for righteousness" into whose keeping and guidance I sincerely commend yourself and all your readers. Haws, Peaketh, March 21st., 1891.
JOHN PEERS.
TILE AUTHORSHIP OF TILE GOSPELS.

Sir,—l now proceed to deal with Lrenteus Papias, and Po'yearn. In his letter of February ',7th, Mr. Dignum asks me to transfer my reading to translations of the Cbristian literature of the second century. He calls attention to Irenwus "who, about A.D. r 77 wrote a work now extant, in which may be read the following pas- sage" :—" Matthew, among the Jews, wrote a gospel in their own language, Mark also the apostle ,and interpre. ter of Peter, delivered to us in writing the things that had been preached by Peter; and Luke the companion of Pacl put down, irk a book the gospel pre-a:Plied by him (Paul). Afterwards John the disciple of the,Lord, who also leahed on his breast, likewlse published a gospel whilst be dwelt in Ephesus in Asia." Mr. Disnum then says hat this testimony goes back to the earlier part of the 2nd oentury—that it is substantially the vary testi- mony of Folycarp, a disciple of John the Apostle, for Irenzeus was a disciple ,of Polycarp. "So that;' says Mr. Dignuni, " between the Apostle St. John and Irenreus there only stands one man from whom Inefreus would receive all information as to the writers of the four gospels." Now this seems very plain sailing' only, unfortunately, it is not so plain as it looks, for it leaves out anything that Polycarp may have told Irenwus. As a matter of fact,we have not a tittle of evidence to show that Polycarp knew anything about the gpels, or that he was even aware of the existence of tha Gospel of John, whose disciple he was. Then how ca a the testi- mony of Irenreus be taken as substantially the testimony of Poly-carp? Irenwus engaged in controversy with certain persons of his time who declined to acknowledge the fourth Gospel. And what does he do? Instead of proving the historical authority of that Gospel by simply stating what he knew about its Apostolic origin, on the tusti • ! mony of Polyearp, the personal disciple of John, he employs the absurd argument that there must be four Gospels because there are four winds. He says, "Since there are four quarters of the viorld in which we are,

div.head: TUE EXAMINER, simuum v. MARCH_ 2S, 1891.
div.p: TUE EXAMINER, simuum v. MARCH_ 2S, 1891.

and four chief winds, the Gospels must be four. Bmides, the Gospel is given by Him who sits above the cherubim, which is a fourfcAd figure, and it answers to the beasts in Rev. IV., which are four,and it must correspond with tiod's covenants through Adam, Noah, Moses, and Christ." Now would Iremeus have resorted to such gro- tesque reasoning as this if he had been in possession of solid historical grounds for the statements he had made? "Not only," says Dr. Martineau, "does he thus disap- point us of his eArly memories when we should be glad to have them; but when at last we get them, they do not prove particularly trustworthy ; for he assures us on the authority of the Gospel and of all the old men in Asia who bad known John, the Lord's Apostle, and of those who had known other apostles besides. that Jesus lived to be more than fifty years of age." It is a remarkable fact that, although he was a disciple of rolycarp, he does not give us a single recital of Polycarp's touching the authorship of the Gospels. His contact and constant intercourse with Polycarp does not in the least enlighten us on the subject, nor does Ile seem to have learned any- thing from him about the composition of the Gospels. Again, whilst he places the four Gospels on the footing of scripture he does the same also with the "Shepard" of Hennas. How much then is his evidence worth?

Now, as to Papias, who was a copious writer, but whose works have all perished. He died about the year 183. Several extracts from his writings have been pre- served by Eusebius, and inthese he tells us that, "Mat- thew wrote the logia, or oracles, in the Hebrew tongue, and everyone interpreted them as he was able "; and that "Mark, ,as the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately,though not in order, all that he remem- bered that was said or done by Christ." "Such lan- guage," says professoeCarpenter, "treats the Evange- ists' narratives as ordinary human literature. The work of Matthew, in the Arammn vernacular of Palestine, was left for each reader to translate as best he could. The feature of Marks's•version of Peter's recollections was its want of proper arrangement, which must, one would think, have impaired the accuracy of the record." This shows that Papias did not view these books in the light of later ideas of inspiration, for he frankly tells us that he attaches more value to oral tradition than to written documents. He says, "1 do not think that I derived as much benefit from books as from the living voice.of those that are-still surviving." It is quite true that in the works of earlier writers Than Papias and 'Tremens passages are to be found that corres- pond with passages in the gospels. Notably is this the case with juStin Martyr. But these writers never men- tion the gospels by name, and, with the exception of the revelations, not a single book in the New Testament is ever referred to by any individual author. This all clearly shows that the gospels as we have them were not 'then known. These early writers only spoke of the Old Testa- ment as Scripture, and the passages they givewhich correspond With passages in the gospels were taken from' what they called the " Memoirs " or " Recollections ' of the Apostles. Professor Carpenter says that these were the sources of Christian teaching; these were the church -books now employed in public worship. Justin Martyr tells us that, "On the day called Sun-day, all who live in the cities or in the country, gather together in one place, and the memoirs of the Apostles, or the writings of the prophets, are read as long as time per- mits."

Several authorities are of opinion that the gospels have been compiled from, possibly, several pre-existinc, works; but that the Gospels are anonymous seems to be con- ceded by almost all authorities, arid that their author- ship is looked upon by Dr. Westcott as a tradition is, I think, clearly proved by tho quotation Mr. Dignum himself has kindly favoured us with. Speaking of the Councils settlina which books were scripture and which were not, he tells us that Dr. Wescott says," The Coun- cils introduced no innovation—but merely proposed to preserve the tradition which had been handed down— ' that is they were merely declarative of what had been received as sacred scriptures in the churches." The italics are mine. Now Ido not possess a copy of Dr. Westcott's book, and I have never read it.tut I have a suspicion that if I did read it I should find other passages very like the one Mr. Dignum has given,and 'should not be surprised to find admissions of a like character in Dr. Lightfoot's book. My friend does not appear to have an abounding faith in Dr. Martineau or Professor Carpenter as authorities, and yet his own authorities,'Dr. Westcott and Professor Beet, are in evident agreement with them that the authorship of the Gospels is a mere tradition. My friend says that the strength of a chain is its weakest link, and he must pardon me if I.point out two extremely weak links in his own chain of argument. First of all, he assures us that the testimony of Irerneus is substantially the testimony of Pelycarp, whereas, we have not a shred of testimony from Polycarp, and no evidence that he knew anything about the Gospels. Se- condly, he tells us on the authority of Dr.'Westcott, that the'Gospels were written by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, and yet in the only extract he,gives us from the doctor's works, we can only infer that their authorship is atradition, since they were only accepted as Scripture by the early church on the strengthuf the tradition which had been handed down.

Mr. Dignum takes strong exception to the monkish legend of the sacred books jumping on the communion table. Does the imbecile logic of Tremens that there must be four Gospels because Were are four winds and four beasts agree with his digestion any better ? He assures me that he finds very solid walks in the regions of ancient ecclesiastical literature. I wish' him much joy of them. shall have at least one more letter to send you in which I propose to deal with the early 'Cirristians. I shall prove my former statements up to the hilt by quotations from Mosheim, Kingsley, and others. My edition of Mosheim is a translation by Dr. Maclaine. and so my friend will understand the want of.verbal agree- ment between his book and mine.—Yours truly, • JOHN GANDY.
GENERAL BOULANGER.

General Boulanger affords a fine example of the instability of political fame. Twelve months ago few men were more spoken of, now "none so poor to do him reverence." Boulanger was born at Rennes in 1837. His mother, who is still alive, was a native of Wales, her maiden name being Griffiths. After an education in the Mili- tary College of St. Cyr, he entered the French army af

a sub-lieutenant. Ile first saw rvice in Algiers, and afterwards took , part in the Franco-Italian war, receiving a wound at the battle of Tarhigo. On the outbreak of the great war against Germany, he had attained the rank of major. He was with Bazaine in Metz, but by some means, escaped the fate of Bazaine's army, and made his way back to Paris. He was actively engaged in the suppression of the Paris Commune, and in 1880 he was appninted to the command of the army of occupation of Tunis. He had a quarrel there with the resident general, and was recalled. He next held the appointment of director of the Infantry Division, and became minister of war in 1886. On the fall of M. Goblet, Boilanger's name did not appear in the Cabinet of M. Rouvier, and he was soon afterwards despatched to Cler- mont-Ferrand to take command of an army corps, receiving a great ovation at Paris on his departure. When the Limousin scandal broke upon Paris like a thunderclap, General Boulanger made some rather free remarks about the War Minister, who imme- diately ordered him under arrest for thirty dteys at his own headquarters. The Government having de- cided, in March, 1888, to cashier the General, he in- augurated a vigorous campaign against the Minis- try._ He won some remarkable electoral victories,

but later on strong action was taken against him by the Government, and he was found guilty 'by the Senate of having appropriated .£lO,OOO of public money, while Minister of War, for purposes-of his own propaganda. He thought it advisable to .flee from France to Belgium and afterwards to England. The General is at present resident in Germany. The falling of a chandelier on General Boulanger's head was announced last year, and " Punch " commented on this incident by saying that it "had shed ad- ditional lustre upon him." Revelations as to the General were published in August by some of his former associates, and as a result of this expose, several duels were fought.
VON AIOLTIKE.

The "first strategist of the day," is as old as the century, having been born on the 26th October, at Parchim, in Mecklenburg. In his twelfth year he went to Copenhagen in order to devote himself, in the bar- racks there, to the military profession. In 1822 he entered the Prugsian service, as a lieutenant in the Bth infantry regiment, and in 1832 he be- came a staff officer. When thirty-five years of age he travelled in Turkey, and was

ltan Mahmoud as to the reor- ganisation of the Turkish army. He remained several years amongst the Turks, and in 1839 he took part in the campaign in Syria against the Viceroy, Mehemed Ali, of Egypt, and his adoptedl son Ibrahim Pasha. On returning to Prussia, his great military abilities were recognised by steady promotion, till, in 1858, he was advanced to the rank of Chief of the Grand General Staff of the Prussian Army. In the Austro-Italian war Moltke was present in the Austrian head- quarters, and after the conclusion of peace he spared no pains that he might fully develop the capacities of the Prussian General Staff and the Prussian army. When the war of 1864 'against Denmark broke out, Moltke sketched the plan of the campaign, and assisted in its execution. In the war against Austria two years later, the whole plan of the Bohemian campaign was due to Moltke, who was personally present in the battle of Konniggratz, which he led, and in like manner ar- ranged the bold advance of the Prussian columns against Olmutz and Vienna, and negotiated the armistice and the preliminaries of peace. To " Father Moltke;" as he is famliarly termed, by the German soldiers, and his brilliant strategy are to be ascribed the splendid victories of the German arms in the Franco-Prussian war, in which he was com- mander-in-chief. From the conclusion of this war till 1889, Von Moltke continued to be chief of the general staff of the German army, but in the latter year he retired from that responsible position. His ninetieth birthday lest October received a national celebration, endives proclaimed a school holiday by the Emperor.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

MANCHESTER COUNCIL AND THE SHIP 'CANAL. A special meeting of the City Council was held on Wed- nesday morning, the Mayor presiding, "to consider, and if thought expedient, to approve of and direct the pro- motion ' of a bill in Parliament for the purpose of enabling the Corporation to render financial assistance to the Ship Canal undertaking and to confer borrowing powers upon the Council. There was a large attendance. The Mayor said the object of the meeting was to give statutory and legal effect to the decision of the Council at its former meeting. They had already given very full; consideration to the whole subject, and he was sorry it had been necessary to call them together again. He did: not intend to re-open thediscussion of the question. He would simply refer to the satisfaction with which the public had endorsed the resolution of the Council. It was most gratifying that the course they were taking had re- ceived such almost unanimous approval from the rate- payers. There would have been nothing to fear if a poll had been demanded except the loss of a month and also • of some money. The majority in .favour of the course they were taking would have been so overwhelming that it'Jnight have strengthened their hands in going for the bill. He had to move the fallowing 'resolution: "That this Council approves of and directs the promotion IV the Mayor, aldermen, and citizens of the City of Man- chester either by thenvolves or jointly with others of a bill in Parliament for Vie pmkpose of enabling the said Mayor, aldermen, and citizens to render financial assist- ance to the Manchester Ship Canal undertaking and to confer borrowing powers upon the said Mayor, aldermen, and citizens and 'for other purposea,in accordance with the report approved and adopted by the Council of the said city on theeth of March,Z69l,and the resolutions then adopted bythesaid Council,or with such modification as Parliament may require."—Sir .John Harwood seconded. The resolution was put and carried unanimously, amid cheers. A rfurther resolution was adopted authorising the affixing ofithe corporate seal to any petition to Parlia- ment which may be necessau for • dispensing with. the standing orders and for obtaining leave to introduce the bill. FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE -SHIPrOANAL WORKS. Mr. Cburton, coroner, held an inquiry at the Queen's Hotel, Frodsham, .on Monday afternoon, touching the death of Charles Gray, a navvy in the employ of the contractors for the Shin Canal. The foreman of the jury was Mr. T. Fletcher, and Mr. Charles C. Henshaw, sub- agent of theFrodsham section., 'were present on behalf of the contractors. Richard Filson, a labourer, in the employ of the con- tractors for the Ship Canal, and wOrking on the Frod- sham section,-said the deceased was a perfect stranger to him, hut was.in the same employ. He was about-. 50 years of age, and had no relations, so far as witness knew, in the district. On Saturday night, he met the deceased near the Weaver Hotel at Weston Point, about half-past eight o'clock, and had at that time a companion with him. They intended to go on to Frodsham Marsh, and all were quite sober at that time.—The Coroner: That is not quite imy experience of another section.— Witness Perhaps not. It was a light night, but the moon was not shining very brightly, Witness and his inaters were making a short cut across the fields to cross the river Weaver, where a gantry was being erected for the passage of engines. The baulk would be a foot in width, and the length attic gantry about 600 feet. It was only in construction, and witness could walk over it without being afraid of his life., Mr. Flenshaw explained that 'from the gantry to the river bed it would be a drop of 16 feet. Another witness said he lodged at the huts, and on Saturday night went to Runcorn, and met with the deceased, who said that there was plenty of time to cross the Weaver befare.the tide came but %when witness and his companions had arrived they saw that it was too high to permit theinto cross the river. Deceased said he could walk over the gantry, and was sober at the time. He had a bundle on his shoulder, which shifted its position when he had gone three parts afthe distance. He was in the act-of putting the bundle right when he overbalanced himself, and fell on to the rock which was being laid, and was instantaneously killed.—The Coroner he had not had the bundle his lifemight not have been lost ?—Witness: I don't think it would.—The Corner: What was the weight of the trundle? It would be about 50 or 60 pounds. —The Coroner:: It fully accounts for it. Mr. Henshaw said that every precaution was taken to provide proper means for the men crossing theriver, and men had no right to cross the gantry. Men were con- stantly kept to work thecboat to convey the workmen across.

The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and Mr. Renshaw observed that when the deceased left the works he was in receipt of Li Bs. 11d. From what transpired after this statement it was shown that there was nothing on the body of the deceased when it .was found but a knife. ANOTHER FATALITY ON THE SHIP CANAL. A shocking aecident, !which has terminated 'fatally., ,occurred to a man named Jones, employed on the Ship Canal works between Weston Point and Runcorn, early fon Tuesday morning. Jones, along with a number of .other men, was pile driving, when the chain of the ponderous hammer snapped and swinging round struck the unfortunate man a violent blow on the head, smash- ingthe skull. The poor fellow was immediately con- veyed on a locomotive to the :Ship Canal hospital at Latehford. Dr. Parker, the resident surgeon, paid every attention to the sufferer, who was in a dying condition *ben ,he was received at the hospital. Dr. Jones, the senior surgeon to the company, was also summoned, but before his arrival death had ensued. Little is at present known 'respecting the deceased, who was apparently about 25 or 26 years of age. An Inquest was held on Thursday. at the Ship Canal Hospital. It appeared that the deceased was engaged in pile.driving operations,and that a portion of his duty was tostilark the piles as they were being driven into the ground, To do this, he had Co stand on axaft closet° the pile driver. The chain— an endless one—was made up of pieces that were screwed together. One of the screws joining the pieces snapped, and in consequence the heavy .chain fell and caught the deceased on the head. He was knocked down like a log, his skull was fractured, and a portion of the brain protruded. 'The poor fellow was conveyed with all possible speed to the hospital at Latchford, where he died in three hours from the time of his admission. Evi- dence was given by fellow-workmen of the deceased, after hearing which the jury found that the cause of death was accidental.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

On Tuesday, before Mr. Handley, Thomas Seaman, Harry Webber, and Martin Moran were each dined as. 6d. and costs for drunkenness. —On Wednesday oe- fore Mr. Handley and Major Hazlehurst, Susannah /eans, an old offender, was sentenced to a month'si hard labour for disorderly,cauduct. She had only been released Isom gaol on the previous day.—Mary Young was fined 10s. and John Kittingham ss. for being drunk.—Joseph Kelly was charged with begging and was discharged with a caution.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—liefore Mr. Brundrit and Dr. Steele.

LICENSES.—Mr. G. W. Cooper, of Wilson's Hotel, ap- plied for an extension of his license on the occasion of S. ball on the 3rd April. Granted until three o'clock. The license of the Grapes. Hotel was temporarily transferred to Emma Field, widow of the late landlord. MAINTENANCE Or A MOTHER.—Edward Richardson was summoned to show cause why he should not contri- bute towards the support of his mother, 70 years of age. who yvas in receipt of ss. per week from the Union.—The defendant had alleged that his mother was the owner of a number of pigs and had private means, but she now came forward and disproved these statersents.—The Bench made an order for s. a week.
DOG AT LARGE.—For this offence George :Oran was fined.ls. and costs.

DRUNKENNESS.—Thomas Bate for being &In* and re- fusing to quit the Manchester House, was fined 10s. and costs. For being drunk andrdisorderly a fine of ss. and osts was impoged upon John I3unlow, Henry Jones, and John Drew.— 7it fine of 2s. ed. and costs was imposed upon Matthew frowey.—Willism Millington was diarged with committing a breach of the peace and he was bound over to be of good behaviour for,six months. YOUNG THIRYRti.—John Fish (a). Wm. Faulkner (13). Thos. Pye<l2), Edward Brannan (8), pleaded guilty to having on Saturday night stolen from the shop door of Walter Collier, grocer, Church-street, three tins of beef and one tio of salmon.—Fish, who had been previously convicted of theft war sentenced to receive 12 strokes ' with the birch rod, •and Faulkner and Pye were sen- tenced to receive six strokes. Brannan was discharged. ASSAULT ON a WIFE.--4Vm. Evans,a sailor,was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assault- ing his wife. On Saturday night the prisoner met his wife in Wellington-street, and asked her for money for drink. She said she had not got any as he had only worked one week since Christmas, and lie struck her a heavy blow between the eyes. The defendant was fined 20s. and costs for the assault and 10s. and costs for the drunkenness, or in default six weeks' hard labour.
DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—Jane Oliver was sent to poi for 14 dAyg for disorderly conduct.

div.head: TOWNSHIP MEETINGS.
div.p: TOWNSHIP MEETINGS.
DUTTON.

The annual, township meeting has been held under the presidency of Mr. Joseph Billington. A number of gen- tlemen were nominated to serve as overseers, and it was resolved to nominate Mi. Thomas Baxter (Dutton Hall), as Guardian of the Poor. Mr. Wm. Fowles was elected waywarden, and Messrs. Sydney E. Stokes. and Daniel Basnett were appointed assessors and collectors of taxes. Messrs. George Kinsey and Peter Priestlier were elected burleymen. Mr. Sydney E. Stokes was re-appointed as- sistant overseer at an increased salary of £4 per annum.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

The. annual meeting of the ratepayers was held on Thursday evening, under the presidency of Mr. E. Aaron. The following gentlemen were nominated for the offices of overseers :—Messrs. E. Aaron, Thos. Ford, Wm. Armstrong, and W. Grounds. Mr. E. Aaron was re-elected waywarden. On the proposition of Mr. J. Blower, seconded by Mr. J. Dunbobbin, the appointment of Mr. Jas. Collier was revoked and determined. On the motion of Mr. Aaron,seconded by Mr. J. W. Kirkham, Mr. Collier was re:appointed at a salary of £6O per annum, being an increase of £l5 per annum. Mr. Aaron ex- plained that 13 years ago when Mr. Collier had his pre- vious increase, the rateable value was only £8,000; now it was £13,000, and the work of the assistant overseer had much increased.

div.head: FR ODSH AAI.
div.p: FR ODSH AAI.

The annual meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Davies, sea. On the proposition of Mr. John Ashtpn, seconded by Mr. H. E. Heywood, a vote of con- dolence with the family of the late Mr. Hedry Linaker was passed. Mr. C. E. Linaker was unanimously elected waywarden, and it was resolved to nominate Mr. John Ashton and Mr. H. E. Heywood as Guardians. The names of Messrs. Davies, F. W. Spencer, and Joseph Edwards are to be submitted for appointment as over- seers. The sum of £l5 was voted to Mr. George Jones, the assistant overseer, for each special sanitary rate Dr. Robinson and Messrs. T. Davies.and H.Tiley were re-elected members of the Parochial Committee. Mr. Ralph Lloyd was re-appointed bellman at the usua salary.

div.head: FRODSHAM LORDSHIP.
div.p: FRODSHAM LORDSHIP.

The Rev. H. B. Blogg presided over the annual town- ship meeting. For the office of wavwarden, there were nominated Mr. Jas. Percival and Mr. J. H. Hargreaves. and after the votes had been counted several times, the Chairman declared Mr. Hargreaves elected. Mr. H. E. Heywood demanded a potion behalf of Mr. Percival, and it was decided that such poll should be taken in the Grammar School, Overton, on Saturday (to-day) from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. Mr. Thomas Lewis was unanimously nominated Guardian, and several persons were selected as eligible to serve as overseers. The sum of £lO was voted to Itilr.,John Challinor, for levying and collecting each sanitary rate. A discussion, without practical result, took placewith regard to the lighting of the township with gas. Messrs. James Percival, R.Bate, and W. C. Collinson were re-elected members of the Parochial Committee.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

The annual township meeting at Penketh was held on Thursday evening, at the Ferry Inn. Mr. Jonas Forster presided. Some discussion took place with reference to the suggestion of the Warrington Gas Committee that gas pipes should be laid to the village, and the Chair- man informed the meeting that those persons who did not wish to have a supply of gas were not hound to take it. The overseers' accounts showed receipts amounting to £452 is. 7d. and an expenditure of £321 16s. td., leaving a balance of £l3O ss. id. in hand. A rate of I.g. in the £ was decttred for the ensuing half-year, ad voluntary rate of in the £, for the purpose of paying jurymen. For the 'offices of overseers Messrs. Jonas Forster, A. Thorpe, and R. Routledge were nominated for •recommendation to the justices. A Committee was ap- pointed to wait upon the lord of the manor and request him to grant the herbage of the recreation ground for the use of the parish.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

The annual township meeting was held in Bethesda schoolroom on Thursday night. The Rev. Canon Wood, Vicar, presided, and there were present Messrs. E. Imison, W. Mellor, W. Jones, T. Jones, W. Hankinson J. K. Digges, G. Moss, J. Lunt, T. Cook, E. Key, W: Betney, Bisbrown, and W. Sutton (assistant overseer). Messrs. Jno. Littler and Thomas Cook were re-appointed auditors of the Burial Board accounts.—The following gentlemen were nominated for the office of overseers : Messrs.S. Taylor, E. Imison, W. Mellor,R. Morris,W. Han- kinson, H. J. Once, J. Pritchard, and W. H. Rogerson. Mr. Imison presented the following statement of ac- counts; receipts; balance to commence with £982 Os. 11d.; April rate is. in the £, £2,721 14s. 6cl. October rate 6d. in the £, £1,828 2s. 10d. ; Ship Canal Company's de- ficiency account, £69 Bs. 2d., bank interest, £9 13s. 9d.; sale of voters' lists, £2 25.; total £5,613 2s. 2d. The payments were as follows :—Justice clerk's fees, 3s. lid; registration of voters, £5B 4s. sd. ; rent, overseer's sal- ary, offices sod expenses, &c., £3ll 14s. id. ; Runcorn Burial Board, £lBO ; Runcorn School Board, £850; Board of Guardians, £3,249 ; which,with a balance of £960 12s. Bd., made the same total as the receipts.

At Stockport, James Royle, labourer, was committed for.trial at the Assizes, on the charge of attempting to murder his wife. The woman had declined to live with him, and it was alleged that be followed her along a lane at Heaton Norris and endeavoured to cut her throat. A boat laden with seaweed has capsized off the coast of Inverness-shire, and a seaman named Donald M'Coll and his two sons were drowned. One bf the keepers on duty at the Ardnamurchan lighthouse saw the boat upset, but was unable to render speedy help. When the boat was reached the lads had gone down, and M'Coll was found lifeless with his arms around the mast.

Mr. T. P. O'Connor M.P., addressing a meeting of his constituents on We Wednesday night at Liverpool, said that if driven to hostility to Mr. Parnell it would be on political and not on personal grounds. There was only one issue in the present struggle,and that was, what was best for Ireland. He condemned Mr. Parnell's mani- festo and his attacks upon Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party.
THE QUEEN ON THE CONTINENT.

MARSEILLES, WEDNESDAY.—Queen Victoria and other members of the Royal party arrived here this morning on their way to Grasse. The Royal train only remained i ten minutes n the station here, during which interval the Briiish consul paid his respects to her Majesty. The Queen was in perfect health, and expressed satisfaction at the manner in which the journey had been per- formed. The Royal train proceeded at eleven o'clock. The public were not admitted to the station during bar Majesty's stay.

It is stated that since the Canadian election the health of the Premier, Sir J. Macdonald, has been failing, and his condition gives the greatest anxiety to his friends.

On Thursday morning, James Thornton, aged 19, and Charles M'Cann, aged 35, were working at the bottom of a sand quarry at Blockhaircl, Glasgow, when a block of freestone, weighing five tons fell and crushed them te death.

The run on the Blackburn Sayings Bank is at an end. On Saturday many depositors were bringing back money they had withdrawn during the panic, and a large number cancelled their notices of withdrawal. Up- wards of £60,000 had been paid out in four days. In the Loudon Bankruptcy Court, on Wednesday, an order annulling the adjudication of Mr. Leslie Fraser Duncan, late of the" Matrimonial News," was made. It was stated that the creditors, with the exception of a few disputed claims, were satisfied.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
PENKETH.
WESLEYA.N CHAPEL EXTENSION.

On Thu.r.s—d-aST evening a meeting for the purpose of exhibiting the revised plans of the chapel exten- sion was held, in the Wesleyan schools. Owing to the plans being late, there were only a few persons present. The plats were ably explained by Mr. It. Cook, and everyone present approved of them.

_ AOCIDENT AT THE TANNERY. A serious accident occurred on Monday morning. at the Penketh Tanning Company's works. A man named Norman was waiting outside to see the foreman, when he was suddenly seized with a fit, and fell to the ground. In falling he received a serious wound in the neck, which bled freely. Several of the workmen who were near observed I the accident, and went to the man's assistance. The local doctor was called in, when it was found he had sustained a severe cut under the chin, about 11 inches long. This was stitched up, and Norman was conveyed home. ACCIDENT IN THE FOOTBALL FIELD. • On Saturday afternoon, whilst the football match between Penketh and Newton Casuals was being played, anfaccident,which might have been attended with serious consequences, occurred to one of the Penketh players, Mr. A. J. Winn. The visiting team, it is said, were somewhat rough in their play, and Mr. Winn, who had just scored, was suddenly charged by one of the Newton men and thrown down, his opponent falling upon him. When they rose from the ground it was found Mr. Winn had sustained some injury to the right arm, as it was hanging useless by his side. He was immediately taken to Dr. Murray, when it was found the elbow had been dislocated. This was at once put right, and he is now progressing favourably.

'in the said 'County, on MONDAY, the 6thday of April next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock ,in the Forenoon. The tearing of all Appeals arising within the Hnndreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield. and Northwich, 'forming the atlas- ford District, and the trials ,of all prisoners committed from such llt-cdreds, will bake place at suchfessions. IN PAISLIAMENT—SESSION 1891. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL (Power to Manchester Ship Canal Company to raise Additional Loan Capital; Extension of Time for com- pletion of the Mancisester Ship Canal and Works; Power to Corporation of Manchester to Lend Moneys to the said ,Company for completion and equipment of Canal Works and for that purpose to borrow additional Moneys ; Pro- :visions as to repayment of moneys to and by the Corpor- ation; Suspension or repeat of power of Company to pay interest on Shares out of Capital during Construction of Worts; Incorporation of Acts; Repeal and Amendment of Acts.) A PPLICATION is intended to be made to the .C-1 House of Commons by Petition as soon as the forms of the House admit by the Manchester Ship Canal Corn pany (hereinafter called the Company) and the Mayor Aldermen and Citizens of the City of Manchester in the County of Lan- caster (hereinafter called the Corporation) or by one of those Bodies for leave to introduce a Bill in the present Session for the following or some of the following among other purposes (that is to say) To enable the Company to raise additional capital by borrowing and by theereation and issue of Debenture Stock. To extend the time limited by the Acts relating to the Company for the completion of the Manchester Ship Canal and Works by those Acts authorised. To empower the Corporation from time to time to lend to the Company such moneys as may be necessary for the com- pletion and equipment of the Manchester Ship Canal and the works connected therewith upon such security terms and conditions as may be defined in the Bill or prescribed by Parliament and to make provision for and in relation to the repayment of such moneys and for the redemption sale or transfer of the securities to be received by the Corporaion from the Company. To extend the borrowing powers of the Corporation and to enable them for the puiposes of the Bill to apply their cor- porate 'funds and any moneys they are already authorised to borrow and to borrow further moneys by mortgage or stock and to charge those moneys on the City Fund and City Rate and all or any funds rates tolls charges and revenues of the Corporation'whether as a Municipal Corporation Sanitary or other Anthority and to make provisions for and in relation to the repayment of the money. To suspendor repeal wholly or partially the power of the Company to pay to their Shareholders interest on their shares out of arum aurinii the remainder of the time for the corn- Didion of the Canal. To enable the Company and aorpOration to enter into and fulfil agreements for or in relation to any of the purposes of the Bill and to confirm any such agreement as may have been already or as during the progress of the Bill may be entered into. The Bill will vary and extinguish all rights and privilegeB which would interfere with any of its objects and will or may incorporate with itself with or without modification any pro- visions thought expedient of the Companies Clausss Consolid- ation Act 1845 the Companies Clauses Act 1863 and the Local Loans Act 1875 and will so far as may be deemed necessary or expedient repeal alter amend or extend the provisions of the Manchester Ship Canal Act 1885 the Manchester Ship Canal Act 1886 the Manchester Ship Canal Act 1837 the Man- chester Ship Canal (Alteration of Works) Act 1888 the Man- chester Ship Canal (Tidal Openings &c.) Act 1890 and the Manchester Sjiip Canal (Various Powers) Act .1890 and any ether Act relating directly or indirectly to the Company and the Manchester Corporation Waterworks and Improye- ment Act 1872 and the Manchester Order Confirmed by the Local Government. Board's Provisional Orders confirmation (No. 11) Act 1886 and any other Act directly or indirectly re- lating to the Corporation. Printed copies of the proposed Bill wili be deposited in the Private Bill Office of the House of Commons if and as soon as leave be given to introduce the Bill and may be ob- tained at the Offices of the undersignlkl. Dated this twenty-sixth day of March 1891. WM. HRNRYNTALBOT, Town Clerk, Manchester. GRUNDY, KERSHAW, SAXON, & SAMSON, 31, Booth Street, Manchester, Solicitors. DYSON & CO., 24, Parliament Street, Westminster, S.W.. Parliamentary Agents.

Robert Jackson and Henry Thornley,. drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-st., on the 22nd, were fined 2s. 6d. each. PITCH AND Toss.—John Cunningham John Mather, J. McKean, and John Henry Lattimore,bOys, were charged with playing at pitch and toss in Ellesmere-St., on Sun- day afternoon. Cunningham and McKean, having been convicted previously, were fined 2s. 6d. each, and the others is. each. CHIMNEY ON FIRE.—John Wm. Powell for having his chimney at the Rope and Anchor Inn, Market-st., on fire, on Sunday afternoon, was fined 2. 6d. THREATENING LANGUAGE.—Jane Hennessy was charged with using threatening language to Sarah Alice Smith, on the 23rd inst. The parties live in Cropper's Brow,and the defendant had threatened the complainant because of her having appeared as a witness against her in the court that morning. She was bound over to keep the peace for six months; in default 14 days' imprison- ment. WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before Major Pickmere. MISCELLANEOUS.—Peter Jones, labourer, and Isaac Watkinsen, slater, both of Warrington, were charged with being drunk and disorderly at Poulton on Sunday night. Sergeant Barnes and P.C. Fleming proved the case, and the prisoners were fined ss. and costa each.—At the same court, on Tuesday morning, before Mr. Stubs, Sarah Ann Lambert was charged by P.C.'s Schofield and McCullagh with being drunk at Rixton that (Tuesday) morning, and was fined ss. and costs. In default of payment, she was committed to gaol for 14 days. •

We give below the returns published by the House of Commons of the attendances of local members in Parliament. Mr. Pickergill's motion for the appointment of a select Com- mittee of inquiry into the increase of betting and gambling, with a view to further legislation, was dis- cussed on the 17th March. It was defeated by a majority of 23. The Welsh Local Optinn Bill, which was not opposed by Government, was carried by six votes on the 18th. There were seveti divisions on the Tithe Bill. DEATH OF THE MARCHIONESS OF DONEGAL. Intelligence reached Belfast yesterday of the death in London of the Dowager Marchioness of Donegal. THE CIVIL WAR IN CHILI. A telegram from Chili has been received in Paris, stating that President Balmaceda has forbidden foreign vessels, and especially British and German vessels, to touch at any port between Charnaraland Arica. A WIFE SHOT DEAD. Mrs. Worrell. wife of an independent gentleman, living at Balmoral House, Matlock Bath, was shot dead late on Thursday night while sitting in an armchair by her own fireside. Mr. Worrell has been arrested on suspicion. THE REPRESENTATION OF WESTHOUGHTON. The Hon. E. G. V. Stanley, eldest son of Lord Stan- ley, of Preston. has been adopted as a candidate for the Westhoughton Division, in room of Mr. F. Hardcastle, M.P., who will resign his seat at the end of the present Parliament. SHOOTING DANCERS IN A BALLROOM. While a charity ball was in progress on Thursday night, at Stryaddy. County Donegal, a man entered the room and discharged a double-barrelled gun at the dan- cers. One girl was shot in the back, and it is feared mortally wounded. The man proved to be insane. THE EASTER MANCEUVRES. The main bodies of volunteers who will be engaged in the operations at Portsmouth, Dover, and other places during Easter, left London on Thursday. The railway arrangements were exceptionally good, and the various battalions arrived at their quarter with commendable punctuality. PROPOSED VISIT OF THE QUEEN TO DERBY. A Derby correspondent states that Mr. Haslam, Mayor of the borough, has received a communication intima- ting that the' Queen will visit Derby on Thursday, May 21, for the purpose of laying the foundation-stone of the new infirmary, which is to be erected at a cost of £75,000, Her Majesty has arranged to pay the visit on her way to Scotland, travelling by the Midland Com- pany's route. hi MR. PARNELL AND THE FIRE ESCAPE. An amusing incident occurred while Mr. Parnell was speaking at his hotel in Sligo, on Thursday night. Some Nationalists rang the fire bell, and, rushing into the sta- tion, said there was a fire at the Imperial Hotel. They obtained possession of the escape, and ran it through the streets to the hotel, placing it against the window of the room in which Mr. Parnell was speaking. Eventu- ally the police, seeing the joke, regained poseession of the escape, which was followed by a jeering crowd to the station.
